After him there was a Tathāgata named Far-Reaching Light; next named Moonlight; next named Sandalwood Fragrance; next named King of Goodly Mountains; next named Sumeru Heaven-Crown; next named Sumeru Equal Radiance; next named Moon-Hued; next named Right Mindfulness; next named Free of Defilement; next named Non-Attachment; next named Dragon Heaven; next named Night Light; next named Peaceful Radiant Summit; next named Immovable Ground; next named Wondrous Vaiḍūrya Flower; next named Vaiḍūrya Golden Hue; next named Golden Treasury; next named Flaming Light; next named Flaming Root; next named Earth-Seed; next named Moon Image; next named Sun Sound; next named Flower of Liberation; next named Adorned Radiance; next named Ocean-Awakening Spiritual Power; next named Water Light; next named Great Fragrance; next named Free of Dust and Defilement; next named Abandoning Weary Thought; next named Jewel Flame; next named Wondrous Summit; next named Courageously Established; next named Merit-Upholding Wisdom; next named Hiding Sun and Moon Light; next named Sun-and-Moon Vaiḍūrya Light; next named Supreme Vaiḍūrya Light; next named Highest Head; next named Bodhi Flower; next named Moon Brightness; next named Sunlight; next named King of Flower Hue; next named Water-Moon Light; next named Dispelling Delusion’s Darkness; next named Crossing the Veil of Conduct; next named Pure Faith; next named Good Dwelling; next named Majestic Spirit; next named Dharma Wisdom; next named Phoenix Sound; next named Lion Sound; next named Dragon Sound; next named Dwelling in the World — all such Buddhas have already passed away.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: Throughout the inconceivable, countless kalpas of the immeasurably distant past, there was a Blossoming Light Tathāgata who appeared in the world, teaching and delivering immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the Way, and then manifesting cessation. After him there was a Tathāgata named Far-Reaching Light, then Moonlight, then Sandalwood Fragrance, then King of Goodly Mountains, then Sumeru Heaven-Crown, then Sumeru Equal Radiance, then Moon-Hued, then Right Mindfulness, then Free of Defilement, then Non-Attachment, then Dragon Heaven, then Night Light, then Peaceful Radiant Summit, then Immovable Ground, then Wondrous Vaiḍūrya Flower, then Vaiḍūrya Golden Hue, then Golden Treasury, then Flaming Light, then Flaming Root, then Earth-Seed, then Moon Image, then Sun Sound, then Flower of Liberation, then Adorned Radiance, then Ocean-Awakening Spiritual Power, then Water Light, then Great Fragrance, then Free of Dust and Defilement, then Abandoning Weary Thought, then Jewel Flame, then Wondrous Summit, then Courageously Established, then Merit-Upholding Wisdom, then Hiding Sun and Moon Light, then Sun-and-Moon Vaiḍūrya Light, then Supreme Vaiḍūrya Light, then Highest Head, then Bodhi Flower, then Moon Brightness, then Sunlight, then King of Flower Hue, then Water-Moon Light, then Dispelling Delusion’s Darkness, then Crossing the Veil of Conduct, then Pure Faith, then Good Dwelling, then Majestic Spirit, then Dharma Wisdom, then Phoenix Sound, then Lion Sound, then Dragon Sound, then Dwelling in the World. All such Buddhas have already passed away.

At that time there next appeared a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja, the Tathāgata — the Worthy One, the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Supreme One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He taught in the world for forty-two kalpas, constantly expounding the sutras and the Way to the gods and to the people of the world.
At that time,

there appeared another Buddha named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata — the Worthy One, the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Supreme One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He taught sentient beings in the world for fully forty-two kalpas, constantly expounding the sutras and the Way to the gods and to the people of the world.
Boundless: without limit or end, describing an extremely long time.

There was a great king of a country named World-Rich King who, hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, rejoiced and understood, and thereupon brought forth the unsurpassed, true intention of the Way. He abandoned his kingdom and gave up his throne, became a śramaṇa, and was known as Dharmākara, cultivating the bodhisattva path.

At that time there was a king of a great country named World-Rich King. Hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, he gave rise to great joy, suddenly awakened, and thereupon brought forth the unsurpassed, true intention of the Way. He then abandoned the throne, shaved his head, and left home, and was known as Dharmākara, cultivating the bodhisattva path.
World-Rich King: the Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment as Spoken by the Buddha (the Han translation) says:

“The Buddha taught the sutras and the Way to the gods and to the people of the world, and none could surpass him. World-Rich King, hearing the sutras and the Way, rejoiced and understood, and thereupon abandoned his kingdom and became a bhikṣu.”

Seeking: in a moment. Śramaṇa: the general term for one who has left home to cultivate the Way. The bodhisattva path: that is, the six pāramitās — the path by which one perfects benefit for self and others and attains the Buddha-fruit. The six pāramitās: the six dharmas by which one may cross from this shore of birth-and-death and affliction to the other shore of nirvāṇa’s peace and bliss — giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and prajñā. Giving overcomes stinginess and greed; precepts overcome transgression; patience overcomes anger; vigor overcomes laziness; concentration overcomes distraction; prajñā overcomes delusion. The details are as in the table below:

Of lofty ability, brave and wise, he transcended and differed from the world; in faith, understanding, clarity, and memory he was foremost in all. He also had supreme vows of practice, together with the powers of mindfulness and wisdom, which enhanced his mind so that it was firm and unmoved. In cultivation and vigor, none could surpass him.

Bhikṣu Dharmākara’s abilities were extraordinary; brave and vigorous, wise and clear-minded, he far surpassed all people in the world. In receiving the teachings with faith, in understanding, in clarity of principle, and in memory, he was foremost in all. He also had supreme vows and aspirations, together with the five powers of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, by which he enhanced his mind, so that before hardship, peril, intimidation, and enticement he stood firm and unmoved. In cultivation and vigor, none could surpass him.

The power of mindfulness and wisdom: here mindfulness and wisdom stand for the five powers. The five powers: the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. The power of faith is the growth of the root of faith, able to destroy all wrong faiths; the power of vigor is the growth of the root of vigor, able to destroy the body’s laziness; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the root of mindfulness, able to destroy all wrong thoughts; the power of concentration is the growth of the root of concentration, able to destroy all deluded imaginings; the power of wisdom is the growth of the root of wisdom, able to destroy all the delusions of the three realms (the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, and the Formless Realm).
He went to where the Buddha was, bowed in homage, knelt long, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and thereupon praised the Buddha in gāthā and brought forth vast vows.
He came to the dwelling place of Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, bowed in homage, knelt long, joined his palms toward the Buddha, praised the Buddha in verse, and brought forth vast vows.
Gāthā: rendered in Chinese as “verse.”
The verse says:

The Tathāgata’s form is wondrous-fair,
in all the world no equal is there.

His light is measureless, illumining the ten directions wide;
the sun, the moon, fire, and jewels all hide
yào, bright
Sun, moon, fire, and jewels all hide their brightness: the light of the sun, the moon, fire, and precious jewels is altogether hidden and unseen.

The World-Honored One sounds but one single note;
each sentient being hears it as befits his lot.

And one wondrous form he can display,
that all beings may see each in his own way.

The World-Honored One can expound with a single sound, yet beings of every kind hear their own language and all understand the principle he sets forth. He can also manifest one subtle form, so that beings of every kind all see the very bodily form of their own kind that pleases them most.

May I attain the Buddha’s voice, pure and clear,
my Dharma-sound reaching all lands far and near.

Proclaiming the gates of precepts, samādhi, and zeal,
and penetrating the Dharma profound, subtle, and real.

Precepts and concentration: this is the abbreviated form of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Precepts, concentration, and wisdom: also called the three trainings, or the three trainings without outflows. Precepts means to stop evil conduct by precepts; concentration means to fix the mind upon one place; wisdom means to break through delusion and realize the truth. Precepts can subdue the mind of greed and craving; concentration can subdue the mind of anger; wisdom can subdue the mind of deluded ignorance. Upholding these three dharmas of precepts, concentration, and wisdom can counteract the three poisons and accomplish the Buddha-fruit; therefore they are called the “three trainings without outflows.”

His wisdom is vast and deep as the sea,
his mind pure within, from affliction free.

He passes beyond the boundless gates of evil fate,
and swiftly reaches the ultimate shore of bodhi, perfect and great.
Free of the dust of toil: without affliction. “Dust of toil” is another name for affliction. The ultimate shore of bodhi: the perfection of Buddhahood.

Ignorance, greed, and anger forever gone,
delusion ended, faults extinguished — by samādhi’s power alone.

And like the immeasurable Buddhas of the past,
for those multitudes a great guiding master, first and last.

“Ignorance, greed, and anger forever gone; delusion ended, faults extinguished — by the power of samādhi”: by the power of samādhi, cutting off forever the greed, anger, and delusion of ignorance, together with the delusions of view and thought, and every fault.

He can rescue every world beneath the sky,
from birth, age, sickness, death, and sorrow’s cry.

Ever practicing giving, precepts, patience, zeal,
vigor, concentration, wisdom — the six pāramitās’ wheel.
The six pāramitās: that is, the six pāramitās, also known as the six crossings.

Those not yet saved, may they be saved and carried o’er;
those saved, may they attain to Buddhahood forevermore.

Though one made offerings to sages countless as the Ganges’ sand,
it were not equal to firm courage seeking the enlightenment-land.

“Those not yet saved, cause them to be saved; those already saved, cause them to attain Buddhahood”: sentient beings who have not yet ended fragmentary birth-and-death are caused to end fragmentary birth-and-death, and sentient beings who have already ended fragmentary birth-and-death are caused to end transformation birth-and-death and attain Buddhahood. Fragmentary birth-and-death: sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, whose lifespans are all limited and whose bodies are all segmented, owing to the retribution of good and evil karma; hence their birth and death are called “fragmentary birth-and-death.” One who has ended fragmentary birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. Cutting off the delusions of view and thought is to end fragmentary birth-and-death — an arhat, for example. Transformation birth-and-death: the sages of the Three Vehicles have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended fragmentary birth-and-death. In the course of cultivating the Way, deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases; each period of this shifting of delusion and awakening differs, and the passage from the earlier period into the later is just like one birth and death, and is therefore called “transformation birth-and-death.” One who has ended transformation birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit. “Though one made offerings to sages countless as the Ganges’ sand, it is not equal to firm courage in seeking perfect enlightenment”: though one made offerings to as many Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it would still not equal one’s own resolute and courageous seeking of the way to Buddhahood, because in this way one can deliver sentient beings all the more. Ganges sand: the Ganges is a great river of India, and its waters hold much fine sand; when the Buddha taught the Dharma, he often used the number of fine sand grains in the Ganges to describe an extremely great number.

May I abide in samādhi’s steady light,
and ever shine my radiance on all, by day and night.

And thus attain a pure abode, vast and fair,
supremely adorned, with nothing to compare.

The vast and pure abode: the pure Buddha-land evoked and manifested when Bhikṣu Dharmākara attained Buddhahood — the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. “Attaining a vast and pure abode”: a Buddha-land is evoked and manifested by a Buddha’s perfect merit, blessing, and wisdom. Beyond all compare: there is nothing that can be compared with it.

All you beings who through the destinies roam,
come swiftly to my land and find peace at home.

Ever with a loving mind I’ll rescue those in distress,
and ferry all the boundless suffering hosts to blessedness.
Pulling beings up: drawing out the suffering of sentient beings.

My resolve is firm, my strength of vow is sure;
only a Buddha’s sage wisdom can know it pure.

Even should this body dwell amid all woe,
this vow-heart of mine shall never backward go.
Gathering in the Buddha-land: to design it concretely and draw up the “blueprint” of the Buddha-land.

When Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this verse, he addressed the Buddha: I am now cultivating the bodhisattva path and have already brought forth the unsurpassed heart of perfect enlightenment; I vow to become a Buddha, altogether like the Buddha. May the Buddha broadly proclaim the sutras and Dharma for me; I shall receive and uphold them, practice as taught, uproot the root of birth and death with all its toil and suffering, and swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

When Bhikṣu Dharmākara had finished speaking this verse, he addressed the Buddha: I now walk the bodhisattva path and have already brought forth the heart of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, vowing to become a Buddha, in all things like the Buddha. May the Buddha broadly proclaim the sutras and Dharma for me; I shall receive and uphold them, practice as taught, uproot the root of birth and death with all its toil and suffering, and swiftly realize the Buddha-fruit (swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment).

When I attain Buddhahood, may my wisdom and radiance, the land I dwell in, and the name of its teaching lord be heard throughout the ten directions. May the gods and people, and creatures that fly and crawl, who come to be born in my land, all become bodhisattvas. If I establish these vows and they surpass those of countless Buddha-lands — can this be attained?

When I attain Buddhahood, may my wisdom and radiance, the Buddha-land I establish (the Western Land of Utmost Bliss), and the name of its teaching lord (Amitabha Buddha) be heard throughout the ten directions. May the gods and people, and even creatures that fly and crawl, who come to be born in my land, all become bodhisattvas. If I establish these vows and they all surpass those of countless Buddha-lands, can this be attained?
Teaching lord
] The Buddha is the lord of the three-thousand-great-thousand world-system that he teaches and transforms.

The name of the teaching lord: that is, the name under which Bhikṣu Dharmākara will become a Buddha (Amitabha Buddha). The land he establishes: that is, the Buddha-land established when Dharmākara becomes a Buddha (the Western Land of Utmost Bliss).

Lokeśvararāja Buddha then spoke these sutra words for Dharmākara: Suppose a man were to measure the great ocean with a bushel, and after passing through kalpas he could still reach the bottom and obtain its wondrous treasures. If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart and does not cease his vigor, he will surely achieve the fruit — what vow could he fail to attain?

Lokeśvararāja Buddha then spoke these sutra words for Dharmākara: Suppose a man were to measure the great ocean with a bushel; after passing through many kalpas he could still reach the bottom and obtain its wondrous treasures. If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart and does not cease his vigor, he will surely succeed — what vow could he fail to accomplish?
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“At that time Lokeśvararāja Buddha, knowing that he was lofty and wise, and that his vows were deep and vast, spoke these sutra words for Bhikṣu Dharmākara: Suppose a man were to measure the great ocean with a bushel, and after passing through kalpas he could still reach the bottom and obtain its wondrous treasures. If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart and unceasing vigor, he will surely achieve the fruit — what vow could he fail to attain?”

Sincere heart: a heart utterly sincere and firm. When such a heart is brought forth, the sage-fruit is necessarily contained within it; because the cause penetrates the ocean of fruition, flower and fruit are simultaneous — one need only be vigorous; what vow could fail to be attained?
Achieving the fruit (kèguǒ):
to succeed.

Reflect for yourself: by cultivating what expedient means can you accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-land? As to how you should practice, you yourself should know. A pure Buddha-land you must gather in yourself.

Reflect for yourself: by cultivating what can you accomplish such an adorned Buddha-land? As to how you should practice, you yourself should know. A pure Buddha-land you should gather in yourself (design it concretely and draw up the “blueprint”).
Cultivating what expedient means: “expedient means” here refers to methods of practice. “Can accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-land”: that you may accomplish the adornment of your Buddha-land.

“You must gather it in yourself”: you should gather it in yourself (design it concretely and draw up the “blueprint”). A Buddha-land is evoked and manifested by a Buddha’s perfect merit, blessing, and wisdom; “Chapter Four, The Causal Ground of Dharmākara” says:
“Thus he attained a vast and pure abode, supremely adorned beyond all compare.”

And first of all, this vast and pure abode, supremely adorned beyond all compare, had to be concretely designed and its detailed “blueprint” drawn. For this, Bhikṣu Dharmākara spent fully five kalpas of time.

Dharmākara said: This meaning is vast and profound, beyond my realm. I only pray that the Tathāgata, the Worthy and Rightly Enlightened One, will broadly set forth the immeasurable wondrous Buddha-lands of all Buddhas. If I may hear such dharmas as these, ponder and cultivate them, I vow to fulfill all my vows.

Dharmākara said: This meaning is too profound; it exceeds my realm. I only pray that the Tathāgata will broadly set forth the immeasurable wondrous Buddha-lands of all Buddhas. If I may hear such dharmas as these, ponder and cultivate them, I vow to fulfill all my vows.

Tathāgata, the Worthy and Rightly Enlightened One: that is, Tathāgata, the Worthy One (arhat), and the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One. Among these, the Worthy One and the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One are the first and second of the Tathāgata’s ten titles.

Lokeśvararāja Buddha, knowing that he was lofty and wise, and that his vows were deep and vast, then proclaimed for him the marks of the meritorious adornment and purity, the vastness and perfection, of twenty-one billion Buddha-lands. In accordance with his heart’s wish, he manifested them all before him. While this Dharma was being taught, a thousand million years passed.

The Buddha Lokeśvararāja, knowing that Dharmākara's wisdom was lofty, bright, and penetrating, and that his vows were deep, far-reaching, and vast, then proclaimed for him the merit, adornment, purity, and vast, perfect fulfillment of two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, the most exemplary of all. And according to his wish he displayed them to him one by one. In setting forth this Dharma, a thousand million years passed.
[That is, he proclaimed for him the lands of two hundred and ten million Buddhas] The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra (Wei translation) says:

“Then the Buddha Lokeśvararāja at once widely proclaimed the lands of two hundred and ten million Buddhas — the good and evil of their gods and humans, the coarse and the sublime of their lands — and in accord with his wish revealed them all to him.

[Thereupon Dharmākara, having heard what the Buddha said and seen it all, gave rise to supreme and peerless vows. Toward the good and evil of those gods and humans and the coarse and sublime of their lands, he pondered to the very end. Then, focusing his mind to oneness, he chose what he desired and brought his great vows to completion.]

At this time, as Dharmākara heard the Buddha Lokeśvararāja set forth each land one by one, and saw each Buddha-land thus revealed, he gave rise to the supreme and peerless vast vow to establish his own Buddha-land. Toward the good and evil of the gods and humans in those two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, the coarse and the sublime of their lands, and all the rest, he pondered and investigated thoroughly. Focusing his mind to oneness, he chose what he himself desired and thereby formed the guiding plan for the land he would establish (brought his great vows to completion).

[With vigor and diligence he sought and searched, reverently and carefully he maintained it, cultivating merit and virtue until he fulfilled five kalpas. Toward the merit and adornment of those two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, he was clear and penetrating, as though they were a single Buddha-land. The Buddha-land he gathered in surpassed them all.]

Then, brave and diligent, he sought and searched with toil, and without slackening cultivated merit and virtue for fully five kalpas, completing the blueprint of the Buddha-land he would establish (embodied in the forty-eight vows). Toward the merit and adornment of those two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, he was clear and penetrating, as though they were a single Buddha-land. And the Buddha-land he would establish surpassed them all.
[The blueprint of the Buddha-land he would establish] The Huishu of the Immeasurable Life Sutra says:
“Now then,
(an opening particle)
a bodhisattva establishes a pure land as a skilled craftsman builds a great city: first he ponders and draws it out.
Five kalpas of pondering — thus he drew it out.”
(Translation: a bodhisattva establishes the Buddha-land he will attain when he becomes a Buddha as a master architect builds a great city: first he thoughtfully draws out the blueprint.
The five kalpas through which Bhikṣu Dharmākara sought and cultivated virtue are exactly the drawing out of the blueprint of his own Buddha-land.)

[Having gathered it in, he again went to where the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja was. He bowed his head at his feet, circled the Buddha three times, and stood with palms joined, saying to the World-Honored One: I have accomplished the pure conduct that gathers in a Buddha-land.]

After Bhikṣu Dharmākara had completed the blueprint of the Buddha-land he would establish, he came once more to the dwelling of the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja. He bowed his head at his feet, circled the Buddha three times, and stood with palms joined, saying to the Buddha: I have accomplished the pure conduct of drawing out the blueprint of a Buddha-land.
[Gathering in] The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra (Wei translation) says:
“May the Buddha widely proclaim the Dharma to me, that I may practice it and gather in a Buddha-land, a pure and adorned land of immeasurable wonder.”

[I have accomplished the pure conduct that gathers in a Buddha-land] After the Buddha Lokeśvararāja proclaimed for Bhikṣu Dharmākara and displayed to him the merit, adornment, purity, and vast, perfect fulfillment of two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, he spent five kalpas drawing out the blueprint of his own Buddha-land (embodied in the forty-eight vows). After he made that blueprint public (set forth the forty-eight great vows), he then piled up merit and accumulated virtue, passing through immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas, and perfectly accomplished the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[He piled up merit and accumulated virtue, passing through immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas, and perfectly accomplished the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss] The preceding text says:

“In ages past, immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas ago, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world, teaching and liberating immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the way, and then entered extinction. Next there was a Tathāgata named Light Far-Reaching, then one named Moonlight, ......, then one named Lokasaṃbhava; all such Buddhas have already passed. At that time there next was a Buddha named the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja.”
“When he set forth this Dharma, a thousand million years passed”
Bhikṣu Dharmākara
) cultivated merit and virtue until he fulfilled five kalpas.”
The later text says:
“Dharmākara became a Buddha, named Amitābha. Since his attainment of Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed to now.”

Therefore the time from Bhikṣu Dharmākara's piling up of merit and virtue to his perfect accomplishment was: immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas, minus the time the fifty-three Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṃkara dwelt in the world, and further minus a thousand million years, five kalpas, and ten kalpas. Seen from the standpoint of modern mathematics, the result is still immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas. Ordinarily, the time for a bodhisattva to cultivate the way and become a Buddha is three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, yet the time for Bhikṣu Dharmākara to cultivate the way and become a Buddha was instead immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas — how many, many, many times more than three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, beyond all reckoning! This shows how immense the difficulty of establishing the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss was — truly inconceivable,
and therefore especially peerless
. Thus Amitābha Buddha is
“the most honored among lights, the king of Buddhas”
, and the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is
“supreme over countless Buddha-lands”

. The most peerless thing about the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss that Amitābha Buddha established is this: other Dharma-gates require one to cut off every affliction (the delusions of view and thought) before one can end birth and death and escape saṃsāra; whereas the Pure Land Dharma-gate needs only ten continuous mindful recitations of Amitābha Buddha at the end of life to move Amitābha Buddha to appear before one and lead one away, so that one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and thereby ends birth and death and escapes saṃsāra (for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth
). Compared, the ease and difficulty of the two are no less than the gulf between heaven and an abyss! Therefore it is said:
“In the Dharma-ending age, of hundreds of millions upon millions who cultivate, scarcely one attains the way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation does one cross over birth and death.”

Moreover, once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one has none of the many sufferings but receives every joy, and at once attains the stage of non-retrogression, until one becomes a Buddha. Therefore the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:

“This question of yours now surpasses in merit a hundred thousand million times the offering of alms to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of one world, and the giving, through kalpas on end, to the gods and humans and to the flying and crawling creatures. Why is that? Because the gods and humans and every living being of the future will all, through your question, gain deliverance from birth and death.”

[Three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas] The time for a bodhisattva to become a Buddha. Kalpas are of three kinds, great, middling, and small; the kalpa spoken of here means a great kalpa, hence “three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas.” As for the number of years in one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, if one reckons ten thousand ten-thousands as one yi and ten thousand yi as one zhao, then one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equals ten million ten-thousand ten-thousand ten-thousand ten-thousand ten-thousand ten-thousand zhao great kalpas.

[The Buddha said: Excellent! Now is precisely the time. You should set it forth in full, to gladden the assembly. And let the great multitude, having heard this Dharma, obtain great and excellent benefit, and be able to cultivate and gather in a Buddha-land, fulfilling their immeasurable great vows.]

The Buddha Lokeśvararāja said with great delight: Excellent! Now is precisely the time; you should set it forth in detail, to gladden the assembly. And let the great multitude, having heard this Dharma, obtain great and excellent benefit, and be able to cultivate how to design their own Buddha-lands, so as to fulfill their immeasurable great vows to become Buddhas and establish lands.

[Excellent] This shows that the conduct of Bhikṣu Dharmākara deeply pleased the sage's mind, accorded with the Buddha's own heart, and broadly responded to the capacities of the assembly; and so he sighed in approval and praised him, saying “Excellent” — these are words of the Buddha's deep delight.
[Dharmākara said: I pray the World-Honored One, in great compassion, to hear and consider.]
Dharmākara reverently said to the Buddha: I pray the World-Honored One, in great compassion, to hear and consider.

[Coveting and reckoning the body] Falsely clinging to a self that has a body (falling into the view of the body), and thereby coveting, reckoning, loving, hating, and judging accord and opposition. In cultivation, ordinary beings mostly fall into the view of the body; the view of the body is foremost among the delusions of view, and unless the delusions of view are cut off one cannot enter the stream of the sages. [Delusions of view] The delusions of view are ordinary beings' errors of confusion in understanding, such as the five wrong views: the view of the body, extremism, wrong views, grasping at views, and grasping at precepts and ascetic practices.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not dwell in the state of the definite assembly and necessarily reach extinction, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

[Concentration] Short for “right concentration.” [The three assemblies] The three assemblies are three classes of sentient beings: the definite assembly (shortened to “concentration”), the wrong assembly, and the indefinite assembly. The definite assembly means those beings who will certainly awaken; the wrong assembly means those who ultimately cannot awaken; the indefinite assembly means those between right and wrong, who may or may not awaken. “even to ten recitations — this is called ten continuous recitations.”

[Roots of virtue] That is, roots of goodness. De means good, ben means root: the merit of every good and ten thousand practices is the root of the Buddha-fruit and bodhi. The Lotus Sutra says:
“At the places of the Buddhas, they plant the roots of every virtue.”
The Immeasurable Life Sutra says:
“Eliminating all outflows, they plant the roots of every virtue.”

[Dedication] “Turning one's own roots of goodness toward some goal” — gathering the roots of goodness one has created and directing them, with added power, toward a certain aim, so that it may swiftly be realized. For example, one dedicates all the good cultivated by one's three karmas (bodily, verbal, and mental) and even such various merits as repentance and entreaty to all beings of the Dharma-realm, that they may together be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth says:
“To dedicate means to turn one's own merit and virtue and bestow it universally upon beings, that together they may see the Tathāgata Amitābha and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Master Shandao's Verses of Vowing to Take Refuge in the Three Treasures say:
“May this merit and virtue be bestowed equally upon all, that together we may give rise to the bodhi-mind and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.”
(The Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles)

[Violet (
gàn
) blue] A color that is red showing through black.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land do not ultimately reach the stage of one more rebirth — except by their own vows, for the sake of beings, donning the armor of the great vow and entering other worlds to freely liberate them all; roaming through the Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva conduct, piling up roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, awakening and transforming sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and establishing them in the supreme true path,
beyond the conduct of the ordinary stages
in succession, and manifesting the practice of Samantabhadra's virtues; if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(22. Vow of One More Rebirth)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas of other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land do not ultimately reach the stage of one more rebirth — except by their own vows, for the sake of beings, donning the armor of the great vow and going to other worlds to freely liberate all beings; roaming through the Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva conduct, piling up roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, and awakening and teaching sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, establishing them in the supreme true path, beyond the conduct of the ordinary stages in succession, and manifesting the practice of Samantabhadra's virtues; if it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[One more rebirth] To finish this one life and then take the Buddha's place — this is another name for the final-body bodhisattva (the bodhisattva of equal enlightenment). For example, the bodhisattva Maitreya now dwelling in the inner court of the Tuṣita heaven is a bodhisattva of one more rebirth. All beings reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss have immeasurable lifespans and in this one life attain Buddhahood; the “one life” spoken of refers to one life of fragmentary birth and death. But the “one life” in “to finish this one life and then take the Buddha's place” refers to one life of transformative birth and death. [Donning the armor of the great vow] They put on the great armor that adorns them with the merit of their vast vows. [Establishing them in the supreme true path] Teaching them to cultivate the Pure Land Dharma-gate. “The supreme true path”

refers to the Pure Land Dharma-gate, for the Pure Land Dharma-gate is perfect and direct, its skillful means ultimate, a single leap straight into the highest and most complete and sudden — and so it is called the supreme true path. Master Hanshan teaches:
“The one gate of the Pure Land embraces all three capacities; the sudden and the gradual alike enter it; no capacity is left out. This is what is meant by transcending the three realms horizontally;
it is the most supreme Dharma-gate
He also teaches:
“Of the Dharma-gates the Buddha taught for cultivating practice and escaping birth and death, there are many skillful means; only Buddha-recitation seeking birth in the Pure Land is
the most swift and essential
(Dream Roaming Collection,
Preface to the Guide to the Pure Land)

[Beyond the conduct of the ordinary stages in succession] Surpassing the practice of the common Dharma-gates that advance step by step in their ordinary order. In the cultivation of the common Dharma-gates, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages from ordinary being to Buddhahood, namely: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dwelling, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten stages of ground, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. But one who cultivates the Pure Land Dharma-gate and is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss sees the Buddha as the flower opens, awakens to the unborn, at once attains the patience with the unborn, and is established in the eighth ground. [The eighth ground] The eighth of the bodhisattva's ten grounds, called the Ground of Immovability. In this ground the bodhisattva dwells in the patience with the unborn, cuts off all exertion, and body and mind are quiescent and extinguished, like empty space; he accomplishes the pāramitā of vow and, with a nirvāṇa mind, is utterly still and unmoving — hence it is called the “Ground of Immovability.” [The ten grounds] The Ground of Joy, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty in Conquest, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Reaching, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Wisdom, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud. These are the fifth set of ten among the bodhisattva's fifty-two stages of cultivation. In these ten grounds one gradually opens the realm of Buddhahood and accomplishes the wisdom of all modes; they already belong to the stage of the sages, and so they are also called the “ten sages.” [The three wisdoms] The wisdom of all, the wisdom of the paths, and the wisdom of all modes. The wisdom of all is the wisdom by which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas understand the universal aspect of all dharmas, the universal aspect being the true nature of all dharmas; the wisdom of the paths is the wisdom by which bodhisattvas understand the various Dharma-gates of cultivation; the wisdom of all modes is the wisdom by which the Buddha penetrates both the universal and the particular aspects of all dharmas and transforms beings and cuts off delusion.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land, relying on the Buddha's spiritual power to make offerings to all Buddhas, cannot in the space of one meal travel to immeasurable, countless millions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(23. Vow of Making Offerings to All Buddhas)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas in my land, relying on the Buddha's spiritual power to make offerings to all Buddhas, cannot in the space of one meal travel to immeasurable, countless millions of millions of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The space of one meal] The time of one meal. The Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom,
Fascicle 347,

Chapter of Entrustment, divides time by length and brevity in turn into: one day and night, one day, half a day, one hour (equal to two hours today), a meal's duration, a moment, a while, and a snapping of the fingers.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land, before all Buddhas, manifest their roots of virtue, and the offerings they require do not accord with their wishes, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(24. Vow That Offerings Follow the Mind)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas in my land, before all Buddhas, manifest their roots of virtue (roots of goodness), and the offerings they require do not accord with their wishes, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Offerings] Also called offerings and gifts: incense, flowers, food and drink, banners and canopies, and other such things offered to Buddhas and bodhisattvas. The Ratnakūṭa Sutra says:
“Bearing
(jī, to carry)
wondrous offerings, they present them to the Tathāgata and to the great assembly.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“In ages to come, with all offerings, they shall make offerings and pay reverence.”
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land cannot expound the wisdom of all, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(25. Vow of Expounding Wondrous Wisdom)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the bodhisattvas in my land cannot expound the wisdom of all, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The wisdom of all] The wisdom that understands the universal aspect of all dharmas; the universal aspect is the true nature of all dharmas.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land, sixteen yojanas in height, do not all gain bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength, if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(26. Vow of Nārāyaṇa Bodies)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the bodhisattvas in my land, sixteen yojanas in height, do not all gain bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength; if it were not so,
then may I not become a Buddha.
The bodhisattvas in my land, sixteen yojanas in height
] The Buddha Speaks of the Great Vehicle Immeasurable Life Adornment Sutra (Song translation) says:

“World-Honored One, when I attain bodhi and accomplish perfect enlightenment, and dwell in my jeweled land, all the bodhisattvas there shall be sixteen yojanas in height and gain the power of Nārāyaṇa. Their bodily marks shall be upright and adorned, their radiance shining, their roots of goodness complete, as they accomplish anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

[Bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength] Their bodies are as firm as adamant and their strength as inexhaustible as that of the god Nārāyaṇa; hence they are called bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land, and all things there, be adorned, pure, luminous, and beautiful, their forms and colors extraordinary, utterly subtle and wondrous beyond all reckoning, and the beings there, even having gained the divine eye, were any able to comprehend and distinguish their names and numbers, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(27. Vow That All Be Adorned and Pure)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the human beings and devas in my land, and all things there, be adorned, pure, luminous, and beautiful, their forms and colors extraordinary, utterly subtle and wondrous beyond all reckoning; and the beings in the land, even having gained the divine eye, were any able to comprehend and distinguish their names and numbers, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Names and numbers]
The number of their names and kinds.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of but scanty merit and virtue, cannot know and see the immeasurable light and color of the bodhi tree, four million li in height, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(28. Vow of Knowing and Seeing the Bodhi Tree)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of but scanty merit and virtue, cannot know and see the immeasurable light and color of the bodhi tree, four million li in height, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land who receive and read the sutras, recite them, uphold them, and expound them do not gain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(29. Vow That Reciting the Sutras Brings Wisdom)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the bodhisattvas in my land who receive and read the sutras, recite them, uphold them, and expound them do not gain eloquence and wisdom, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land can be measured or limited, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(30. Vow of Unlimited Wisdom and Eloquence)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land can be measured or limited, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and my land be pure, so that it reflects and reveals all the immeasurable, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as a bright mirror reveals the face — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(31. Vow of Reflecting the Ten Directions)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and my land be pure, so that it reflects and reveals all the immeasurable, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as in a bright mirror one sees (beholds) the face. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and from the ground up to the empty air — palaces, towers, ponds, streams, flowers, and trees, and all the myriad things in my land — all be compounded together from immeasurable jewels and fragrances, adorned with wondrous beauty surpassing that of gods and humans, their fragrance pervading the worlds of the ten directions, and the bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the Buddha's conduct — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(32. Vow of Wondrous Adornment with Jewels and Fragrance)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and from the ground up to the empty air — palaces, towers, ponds, streams, flowers, and trees, and all the myriad things in my land — all be compounded together from immeasurable jewels and fragrances, adorned with wondrous beauty surpassing that of gods and humans, their fragrance pervading the worlds of the ten directions, and the bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the Buddha's conduct. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, touched in body by my radiance, are not made soft in body and mind, surpassing gods and humans — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(33. Vow That Those Touched by the Light Be Made Soft)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, touched in body by my radiance, are not made soft in body and mind, surpassing gods and humans. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name do not gain the bodhisattva's patience with the unborn and all profound dhāraṇīs, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(34. Vow That Those Who Hear the Name Gain Patience)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name do not gain the bodhisattva's patience with the unborn and all profound dhāraṇīs, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Patience with the unborn] Shortened to “patience with the unborn”: penetrating that all dharmas are fundamentally unborn, that sentient and insentient alike arise from conditions and have no nature of their own, and are in their very substance empty; and therefore dwelling at peace in the unborn Dharma without the mind stirring. [No nature of their own] Nature means substance; all dharmas have no substantial entity (and so are illusory), which is called having no nature of their own. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Knowing that all dharmas are ever without a nature of their own.”
The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“All illusions become without a nature of their own.”
[Dhāraṇī]
Upholding all dharmas, so that good dharmas are not lost and evil dharmas do not arise.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and in my land there be women; should women wish to be born in my land, they at once become men; and the countless gods and humans, and even the flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotus flowers in ponds of seven jewels, and when grown are all bodhisattvas and arhats — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(35. Vow of No Women and Lotus Birth)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and in my land there be women; should women wish to be born in my land, they at once become men; and the countless gods and humans, and even the flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotus flowers in ponds of seven jewels, and when grown are all bodhisattvas and arhats. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[That in my land there be women]
The Buddha Speaks of the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, the Sāl Tree, and Deliverance from the Human Path (Wu translation) says:

“The second vow: when I become a Buddha, let there be no women in my land. Should women wish to come to be born in my land, they at once become men. The countless gods, humans, and flying and crawling creatures who come to be born in my land shall all be born by transformation in lotus flowers in ponds of seven jewels. When grown they shall all be bodhisattvas and arhats, countless in number. If I gain this vow, then I shall become a Buddha; if I do not gain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.”
The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Sutra (Han translation) says:

“In that land all are bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and lifespans are exceedingly long, measureless countless kalpas. Women who are reborn there are born by transformation and all become men.”
[Countless] Without end.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, after the end of their lives, always cultivate the pure conduct until they attain the Buddha-way — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(36. Vow of Always Cultivating Pure Conduct)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, after the end of their lives, always cultivate the pure conduct until they attain the Buddha-way. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Pure conduct]
Pure and undefiled action.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the gods and humans of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, throw themselves to the ground with the five limbs, bow their heads in reverence, rejoice in joyful faith, and cultivate the bodhisattva conduct, and the gods and people of the world do not all do them reverence — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(37. Vow That Gods and Humans Do Reverence)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the gods and humans of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, throw themselves to the ground with the five limbs, bow their heads in reverence, rejoice in joyful faith, and cultivate the bodhisattva conduct, and the gods and people of the world do not all do them reverence. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land wish to obtain clothing
(garments and adornment)

and it comes at once with the thought; as the Buddha praises, wondrous garments according with the Dharma are naturally on the body; and if there be any cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(38. Vow That Wondrous Garments Follow the Thought)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the human beings and devas in my land wish to obtain clothing, and it comes at once with the thought, as the Buddha praises, wondrous garments according with the Dharma naturally on the body; and if there be any cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land receive a happiness not equal to that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(39. Vow of Joy Like That of the Outflow-Exhausted)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land receive a happiness not equal to that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Outflows exhausted] Having cut off every affliction (the delusions of view and thought). Outflow is another name for affliction. [The delusions of view and thought] The delusions of view and the delusions of thought. The delusions of view are ordinary beings' errors of confusion in understanding, such as the five wrong views: the view of the body, extremism, wrong views, grasping at views, and grasping at precepts and ascetic practices; the delusions of thought are ordinary beings' errors of confusion in thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root of sentient beings' birth and death through saṃsāra; cut them off and one can end birth and death and escape saṃsāra.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land who, as they wish, desire to see the immeasurable, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, do not at once have their wish fulfilled, seeing them all reflected in jewel trees as in a bright mirror one sees the face — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(40. Vow of Lands Appearing in Trees)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas in my land who, as they wish, desire to see the immeasurable, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, at once have their wish fulfilled, seeing them all reflected in jewel trees as in a bright mirror one sees the face. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should, until they become Buddhas, be deficient or incomplete in any of their faculties, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(41. All Faculties Complete)
If I become a Buddha,
and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should, until they become Buddhas, be deficient or incomplete in any of their faculties, then I shall not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should all fail to obtain the samādhi of purity and liberation; and if, dwelling in that samādhi, in the space of a single thought they should fail to make offerings to immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, without losing their concentration — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(42. Dwelling in Samādhi, Making Offerings to Buddhas)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should fail to obtain the samādhi of purity and liberation — dwelling in that samādhi, in the space of a single thought making offerings to immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, without losing their concentration — then I shall not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should, after the end of their lives, fail to be born into noble families — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(43. Hearing the Name, Attaining Blessings)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should after the end of their lives fail to be born into noble families — if this should not be so, then I shall not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should not leap with joy, cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and perfect the roots of virtue — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(44. Perfecting the Roots of Virtue)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should not leap with joy, cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and perfect the roots of virtue (roots of goodness) — if this should not be so, then I shall not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should all fail to obtain the samādhi of universal equality; and if, dwelling in that samādhi, until they become Buddhas, they should fail constantly to behold immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(45. The Samādhi of Universal Equality)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should all fail to obtain the samādhi of universal equality — dwelling in that samādhi, until they become Buddhas, constantly beholding immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas — then I shall not become a Buddha.
[The samādhi of universal equality] One who cultivates this concentration can, within that samādhi, behold all Buddhas everywhere.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows, should fail to hear at will the Dharma they wish to hear — if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(46. Hearing the Dharma According to One's Vow)
If I become a Buddha,
and the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows, should fail to hear at will the Dharma they wish to hear — if this should not be so, then I shall not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should fail immediately to attain non-retrogression — may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(47. Hearing the Name, Attaining Non-Retrogression)
If I become a Buddha,
and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should fail immediately to attain the stage of non-retrogression, then I shall not become a Buddha.
[The stage of non-retrogression] Also rendered as avaivartika, or as Apidha (
pí

)bazhi — that is, Aparivartya. This is the name of a bodhisattva stage. A bodhisattva must cultivate for one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa before he can reach this stage. From that point on there is only advance, step by step, until Buddhahood; in between there is no falling back. The Sutra of Amitābha Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha, says:
“The sentient beings who are born in the Land of Utmost Bliss are all avaivartika.”

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters who hear my name should fail immediately to reach the first, the second, and the third Dharma-patience, and should be unable immediately to attain non-retrogression with respect to all Buddha-Dharmas — may I not attain perfect Enlightenment.
(48. Attaining the Three Dharma-Patiences)
If I become a Buddha,

and the bodhisattvas in the lands of other quarters, hearing my name, should fail immediately to reach the first, the second, and the third Dharma-patience, and should be unable immediately to attain non-retrogression with respect to all Buddha-Dharmas, then I shall not become a Buddha.

[The first, the second, and the third Dharma-patience] Namely, the patience of sound and echo, the patience of gentle compliance, and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. For a detailed commentary on these three kinds of patience, see “15. The Bodhi Site.”
[The Buddha told Ānanda: Then the bhikṣu Dharmākara, having spoken these vows, spoke in gāthās:
I establish a resolve surpassing the world,
(I must fully realize the fruit of Buddhahood)
and if these vows are not fulfilled
(if these forty-eight vows are not fulfilled)
, I swear I shall not attain perfect Enlightenment
(I swear I shall not become a Buddha)

[A resolve surpassing the world] This is the resolve spoken of earlier: “surpassing the lands of countless Buddhas.” [Perfect Enlightenment] True awakening; becoming a Buddha is called attaining perfect Enlightenment. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“The Buddha told Ānanda: When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this gāthā, he addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘Just so, World-Honored One! I have brought forth the mind of unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment. May the Buddha broadly proclaim the Dharma of the scriptures for me; I shall cultivate accordingly and gather in a pure and adorned, immeasurable, wondrous Buddha-land. Grant that in this world I may swiftly attain perfect Enlightenment and uproot the very source of the toil and suffering of birth and death.’”
Again, as a great donor I shall relieve all who are poor and suffering, and cause all those multitudes of beings to be free from sorrow and affliction through the long night.
Bringing forth all roots of goodness and accomplishing the fruit of bodhi — when I attain perfect Enlightenment, my name shall be Immeasurable Life.
[Immeasurable Life] This is a Buddha's name; its transliteration is Amita.
When beings hear this name
(when beings hear this name and title)
, they all come to my land; their bodies are of the Buddha's golden hue, and all their marvelous marks are complete.
And with a heart of great compassion they benefit all the multitudes of beings,
(causing them)
to leave desire behind, to dwell in profound right mindfulness, and to cultivate the pure conduct of the holy life with pure wisdom.
[Multitudes of beings] Sentient beings.
May the light of my wisdom universally illumine the lands of the ten directions, dispelling the darkness of the three defilements and rescuing beings from all their woes.

[The three defilements] Another name for the three poisons, namely greed, hatred, and delusion. [The darkness of the three defilements] The darkness of the three poisons. [Rescuing beings from all their woes] Rescuing sentient beings from all their woes by the light of wisdom.
Causing all to renounce the sufferings of the three evil paths, to extinguish the darkness of the afflictions, to open the eye of wisdom for them, and to gain the body of light.

[The three paths] The path of blood, the path of knives, and the path of fire. The path of blood is the animal realm, because animals dwell where they are constantly killed or devour one another; the path of knives is the realm of hungry ghosts, because hungry ghosts dwell where hunger and the coercion of swords, whips, and staves are constant; the path of fire is the hell realm, because hells are places of constant freezing cold or of scorching by fierce fire. These three paths are another name for the three evil paths.
Shutting off
(closing)
all evil paths, opening up
(throwing open)
the gate of good destinies, opening the Dharma-treasury for the multitudes, and bestowing abundantly the treasure of merit and virtue.

[Evil paths] As the world's people understand it, the evil paths are the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; but the evil paths spoken of here are the five evil paths named in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) — hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. “Shutting off all evil paths” means cutting off the road of birth-and-death transmigration. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“Each should diligently and vigorously strive, and seek it for himself with all his might. He will surely transcend and pass beyond, and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Cutting across the five evil paths, the roads of those destinies are naturally closed.”

[The five evil paths] Namely: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. Because these five paths are the road of birth-and-death transmigration, for a cultivator who would end birth and death and escape the three realms they are all evil paths.
[Good destinies] “Good destinies” here does not mean the three good paths among the six paths (gods, humans, and asuras), but rather the ending of the road of birth-and-death transmigration.
[Opening the Dharma-treasury for the multitudes] Teaching sentient beings to reveal their own intrinsic nature (the Dharma-treasury).

[Dharma-treasury] Also called the treasury of Buddha-Dharmas, or the Tathāgata-garbha; that is, the intrinsic nature of sentient beings, which contains and holds all the merits of the Tathāgata's fruition-ground. (See in full
“Heart, Intrinsic Nature, Tathāgata-garbha”
Like the Buddha's unobstructed wisdom, practicing deeds of kindness and compassion, always acting as teacher of gods and humans, and becoming the hero of the three realms.
Proclaiming the Dharma with a lion's roar, broadly delivering all sentient beings, fulfilling the vows made in the past
(perfectly accomplishing the forty-eight great vows made in former days)
, and causing all to become Buddhas
(causing all beings born in my land to become Buddhas)

[The lion's roar] The Buddha proclaims the Dharma without the least fear, his voice shaking the ten directions, so that all demons are awed into submission — as when the lion roars and a hundred beasts submit.
[All becoming Buddhas] Causing all sentient beings born in my land to become Buddhas. This is as the forty-eight vows above say:

“All sentient beings, and those in the realm of Yama, and those in the three evil paths, who come to be born in my land and receive the transforming influence of my Dharma, shall all accomplish anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
If these vows attain their fruit
(if these vows are to be accomplished)
, the great chiliocosm should tremble in response
(the great chiliocosm should tremble in response)
, and all the gods of the heavens should rain down rare and wondrous flowers.]

[The Buddha told Ānanda: When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this gāthā, the whole earth immediately trembled in six ways. The heavens rained wondrous flowers, scattering them upon him. Music sounded of itself in the air, with voices of praise saying: He is certain to attain unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this gāthā, the whole earth immediately trembled in six ways. The heavens rained wondrous flowers as if falling rain, scattering them upon him. Music sounded of itself in the air, with voices of praise saying: He is certain to attain unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment (he is certain to become a Buddha).

[The six kinds of trembling] The six signs of auspicious trembling, namely: moving, surging, quaking, striking, roaring, and bursting. These six kinds of trembling can be known and seen only by one who has the divine eye; ordinary beings know nothing of them. [The voices of praise in the air: He is certain to attain unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment] Because the bhikṣu Dharmākara declared in his forty-eight vows: if any one of these vows is not fulfilled, I swear I shall not become a Buddha. “The voices of praise in the air: He is certain to attain unsurpassed perfect Enlightenment” is a prophecy: the bhikṣu Dharmākara will certainly become a Buddha, and all forty-eight vows will be fulfilled.
This chapter teaches: the bhikṣu Dharmākara, through cultivation over immeasurable kalpas, accumulated merit and virtue, and thereby brought forth the Buddha-land (
“sensing and attaining a vast and pure dwelling-place”
) — the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.

[Ānanda, when the bhikṣu Dharmākara had brought forth these vast and mighty vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, and in the midst of all the multitudes of gods and humans, he dwelt in true wisdom, courageous and vigorous, single-mindedly and devotedly adorning the wondrous land. The Buddha-land he cultivated was open and vast, supreme and uniquely wondrous, established and ever constant, without decay or change.]

Ānanda, after the bhikṣu Dharmākara had brought forth these forty-eight great vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja and in the midst of all the multitudes of gods and humans, he dwelt in true wisdom and cultivated with courage and vigor, always single-mindedly and devotedly adorning the Buddha-land (the wondrous land) with the immeasurable, boundless merits of the fruition of awakening. The Buddha-land he was to cultivate was open and broad, magnificent and vast, supreme and uniquely wondrous, altogether foremost. It is ever constant and unchanging, never decaying or growing old.

[The Buddha-land he cultivated] The Buddha-land he cultivated was brought forth and made manifest by the immeasurable, boundless merits of the fruition of awakening of the bhikṣu Dharmākara. The Vajraśekhara Sutra says:
“This Buddha-land alone is made entirely pure by the vajra-nature itself.”
[Established and ever constant, without decay or change] The Buddha-land he cultivated (the Land of Utmost Bliss), once established, is forever thus; it has no marks of decay or damage.

[Through immeasurable kalpas, he accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, hatred, delusion, or desire, and was unattached to sights, sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects. He delighted only in recollecting the roots of goodness cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the practice of stillness, far removed from falsehood. Relying on the gate of ultimate truth, he planted the roots of all virtues, counting no hardships.]

Through immeasurable kalpas the bhikṣu Dharmākara accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, hatred, delusion, or desire, nor was he attached to the objects of the six dusts. He delighted only in recollecting the goodness cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the practice of stillness, far removed from falsehood. Relying on the gate of ultimate truth, he cultivated the roots of all virtues, counting no hardship or difficulty as too great.
Through immeasurable kalpas, he accumulated and planted virtuous conduct
] The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:
“Through inconceivable koṭis of kalpas, he accumulated and planted the immeasurable virtuous conduct of a bodhisattva.”

A bodhisattva needs only three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas to become a Buddha, yet the bhikṣu Dharmākara passed through immeasurable kalpas before completing the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. From this we can see how great the difficulty was — and therefore how incomparably supreme the Western Land of Utmost Bliss is! [The six dusts] The dust of form, the dust of sound, the dust of scent, the dust of taste, the dust of touch, and the dust of mental objects. “Dust” means defilement; it is so called because it can defile the human mind and prevent the true nature from manifesting. It is also called the six objects, the outer objects perceived by the six sense-faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). [Ultimate truth] The true principle of the stillness of nirvāṇa as seen by sagely wisdom is called ultimate truth.

[Having few desires and knowing contentment, he sought only the pure Dharma and benefited the multitudes of beings. His resolve never flagged, and his power of patience was perfected. Toward all sentient beings he always bore kindness and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words he exhorted, instructed, and urged them on. He reverenced the Three Jewels, served his teachers, and had no heart of falseness or flattery.]

He had few desires and knew contentment, seeking only the good Dharma and benefiting the multitudes of beings. His resolve never flagged, and his power of patience was perfected. Toward all sentient beings he always bore kindness and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words he exhorted, instructed, and urged them on. He reverenced the Three Jewels and served his teachers, without any heart of falseness or flattery.
[Pure Dharma] The general name for all good dharmas. [The power of patience] The power of patient endurance. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Again I see the Buddha's disciples dwelling in the power of patience; when arrogant people revile and beat them, they are able to endure it all, seeking the Buddha-Way.”
[Kindness and patience] Compassion and patient endurance. [Exhort and instruct] To admonish and to make clear. [Urge them on] To encourage and cause them to advance.

[Adorning all practices, his norms and models were complete. He contemplated all dharmas as illusory transformations, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded his mouth-karma well and did not ridicule the faults of others; he guarded his body-karma well and did not transgress the precepts and rules; he guarded his mind-karma well and was pure and undefiled. To all lands, cities, settlements, kin, and treasures he was wholly unattached. Constantly, by giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom — the practices of the six pāramitās — he taught, established, and settled sentient beings in the unsurpassed, true Way.]

The bhikṣu Dharmākara adorned all practices, and his norms and models were complete. He contemplated all dharmas as illusory transformations, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded his mouth-karma well and did not ridicule the faults of others; he guarded his body-karma well and did not transgress the precepts and rules; he guarded his mind-karma well and was pure and undefiled. To all lands, cities, settlements, kin, and treasures he was wholly unattached. Always, by giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom — the wondrous practices of the six pāramitās — he taught, established, and settled sentient beings, causing them to dwell in the unsurpassed, true Way.

[Norms and models] The standard that conduct ought to follow. [Contemplating all dharmas as illusory transformations] Contemplating all dharmas as being like magical illusions. [Precepts and rules] The precepts are the moral code; the rules are the ceremonial norms — what a cultivator must follow in establishing himself and dealing with the world.

[Because he accomplished such roots of goodness, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures naturally appeared in response. Sometimes he was an elder or a householder, of a wealthy clan and honored estate; sometimes a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage emperor; sometimes a lord of the six heavens of desire, and even a Brahmā king. In the presence of all Buddhas he honored and made offerings without ever ceasing. Such merit as this cannot be fully told.]

Because the bhikṣu Dharmākara accomplished such roots of goodness, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures welled up naturally. In his successive lives he was sometimes an elder or a householder, of a wealthy clan and honored estate; sometimes a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage king; sometimes a lord of the various heavens of the realm of desire, and even the great Brahmā king of the realm of form. In the presence of all Buddhas he honored and made offerings without ever ceasing. Such merit as this cannot be fully told.

[Immeasurable treasures naturally appeared in response] Because the bhikṣu Dharmākara accumulated over many kalpas the merit of giving and of keeping the precepts, treasures appeared in response, welling up naturally. [Elder] A general term for one who has accumulated wealth and possesses virtue. [Kṣatriya] That is, kṣatriya, the second of the four Indian castes. [The four castes] Brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra. The brāhmaṇas were the priests of ancient India and held the highest authority; the kṣatriyas were the royal class, honored as were the brāhmaṇas; the vaiśyas were the ordinary class of workers, farmers, and merchants; the śūdras were slaves who served others. [The six heavens of desire] The realm of desire (the world in which beings dwell who have the two desires of lust and food) has six heavens, hence the name: the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, and the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others' Transformations. [Lord of the six heavens of desire] The lord of each heaven of the realm of desire. [Brahmā king] An abbreviation of Great Brahmā King. [The realm of form] Above the realm of desire. Because the beings of this realm have only a physical body and are free of the two desires of lust and food, it is called the realm of form.

[Sometimes a lord of the various heavens of the realm of desire, and even the great Brahmā king of the realm of form] The Sutra of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life and Adornment (the Song translation) says:
“Ānanda, the monk Dharmākara
(the bhikṣu Dharmākara)

, when he practiced the bodhisattva practices, honored and reverenced and made offerings in the presence of all Buddhas without ever ceasing. As a great king of the Four Heavens, he constantly went to the Buddha's presence, reverently bowing and making offerings. As a king of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, he constantly went to the Buddha's presence, reverently bowing and making offerings. As a king of the Yāma Heaven, a king of the Tuṣita Heaven, a king of the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, a king of the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others' Transformations, and even as a great Brahmā king, he constantly went to the Buddha's presence, reverently bowing and making offerings.”
[From body and mouth there constantly came immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like sandalwood
(zhān)

and the utpala flower; its fragrance universally perfumed immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his countenance was dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty subsidiary characteristics were all complete. From his hands there constantly came inexhaustible treasures, adornments, and all necessities — the very finest things — bringing benefit and joy to sentient beings. By this cause and condition he was able to cause immeasurable sentient beings all to bring forth the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.]

By the response of his merit, from the body and mouth of the bhikṣu Dharmākara there constantly came of themselves immeasurable wondrous fragrances, like sandalwood and the utpala flower, whose fragrance universally perfumed immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his countenance was dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty subsidiary characteristics were all complete. From his hands there constantly came inexhaustible treasures, adornments, and all necessities — the very finest things — to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings. By this cause and condition he was able to cause immeasurable sentient beings all to bring forth the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

[The eighty subsidiary characteristics] Also called the eighty minor marks, namely: an invisible uṣṇīṣa; a high nose without visible nostrils; eyebrows like the new moon; ear-lobes hanging down; a body firm and solid as Nārāyaṇa's; joints like hook and chain; the body turning at once like an elephant king's; when walking, the feet raised four inches from the ground, leaving an imprint; nails the color of red copper, thin and lustrous; knee-bones firm, round, and fine; a clean body; a soft body; an unbending body; fingers round and slender; the lines of the fingers hidden; veins deep and invisible; ankles invisible; a lustrous body; the body self-possessed and not bent; a full and complete body; a complete and sufficient countenance; an abiding-place so stable that none can disturb it; majesty shaking all; all beings rejoicing to see him; a face neither long nor large; a countenance upright and unfaltering in color; face and eyes complete; lips the color of the bimba fruit; a voice deep and far-reaching; a navel deep, round, and fine;
