Free of craving and greed, their vows are settled and firm. They neither add nor diminish, seeking the Way in harmony and uprightness. Undeceived by crooked views, they follow the sutras and keep the precepts. They dare not stumble or slip, as though measuring by the inked line. All aspire to the Way, vast and free of other thoughts. Free of care and sorrow, naturally unconditioned. Like empty space, they stand on nothing; calm and at peace, they have no desires.

They have no craving or greed, and their vows are firm. They are not now hot and now cold (neither adding nor diminishing), but seek the Way in harmony and uprightness. Undeceived by biased views and false teachings, they strictly follow the words of the sutras and the precepts (following the sutras and keeping the precepts). They dare not make the slightest error, like a carpenter following the inked line. They aspire with all their strength to the supreme Way, and their minds are vast and empty of deluded thoughts. Free of care and sorrow, naturally unconditioned. Their minds are like empty space, in which not a single dharma is established; calm and at peace, they have no desires.
Craving and greed: to be steeped and stained is craving. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"Know that cyclic existence has craving as its root."
To desire and seek is greed.
The Lotus Sutra says:
"Craving and desire are the root of all suffering; if craving and desire are extinguished, there is nothing left to rely on
(the causes of suffering have no support)
The inked line: a carpenter dyes a cord with ink and snaps it against a plank to mark a straight line, by which he saws and planes. It is a simile for rules and standards.

The next two passages describe the state of those in the Land of Ultimate Bliss who have understood the mind and seen the nature. To understand the mind and see the nature (to perceive the nature thoroughly) is what the Chan school pursues with unflagging zeal: it is extremely difficult and few ever succeed. Yet for those born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss it comes as a matter of course, without a single exception. Therefore Master Yongming, in his Four Selections, says:
"If only one sees Amitabha, why worry that one will not awaken
(understand the mind and see the nature)

They make good vows and seek with all their hearts. With grief-borne compassion they fully accord with propriety and righteousness, embracing both the outer and the inner, and cross over into liberation. Naturally they preserve and protect themselves, utterly true and utterly white, their vows supreme, in pure samadhi and peace.

They make good vows and seek with all their hearts. With great compassion (grief-borne compassion) they fully accord with worldly propriety, law, and righteousness; principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused (embracing the outer and the inner), and they attain liberation. Freely and naturally they protect their own mind-nature; not a single thought arises (utterly true and utterly white), their vows are supreme, and they dwell in pure samadhi and peace.

Good vows: that is, what was said earlier in "26. Making Offerings, Hearing the Dharma": "Their resolve seeks to adorn the Pure Land (taking Amitabha Buddha as their teacher, they resolve to obtain a Buddha-land as adorned and pure as the Land of Ultimate Bliss)."
Making good vows and seeking with all their hearts: "5. Supreme Aspiration and Diligent Progress" says:
"They formed great vows and sought with diligent zeal."

Embracing both the outer and the inner: "outer" refers to the marks of phenomena, "inner" to the essence of principle. To embrace both outer and inner is to perfect both principle and phenomena. Crossing over: the meaning is to be ferried across to liberation. The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure Equality and Enlightenment (Han translation) says:

"The heavenly and human beings of the eight directions, above and below, throughout the world, whom it ferries across — even the fliers and creepers and wrigglers — are all caused to attain the Buddha's path of nirvana."

Once one opens through to clarity, the natural within the natural shows its natural aspect, and the natural has its root. Naturally it forms five lights, the five lights transform into nine colors; the Shen
shēn

star wheels and the Dipper turns, with hundreds and thousands of transformations — the most supreme naturalness. Naturally it forms the seven treasures, gathering them across into all things; the light, essence, and brightness all emerge together, excellent and good beyond all compare. It abides in neither above nor below, penetrating without limit.

Once one suddenly opens to awakening (understanding the mind and seeing the nature), one beholds the natural aspect within the natural (no longer distorted by one's own outlook, emotions, or feelings), and the natural (this naturally manifested myriad phenomena) has its root (the true nature of all dharmas). The natural aspect becomes five lights, the five lights become nine colors, the Shen star wheels and the Dipper turn, with hundreds and thousands of transformations — the most supreme naturalness. This most supreme naturalness in turn transforms into the seven treasures, gathering them across to form all things,
with subtle light shining forth in splendor,
beyond all compare. No longer clinging to distinctions of above and below, pure and impure, and the like, one penetrates all things without limit.
Opening through to clarity: understanding the mind and seeing the nature, that is, perceiving the nature thoroughly. On self-nature and Buddha-nature, see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
. The Shen (
shēn
) star wheels and the Dipper turns: a simile for unceasing transformation. Shen is the Shen star, the brightest star of the northern winter sky; the Dipper is the Northern Dipper.
Abides in neither
above nor below
no longer clinging to distinctions of above and below, pure and impure, and the like. The Diamond Sutra says:
"This Dharma is equal; there is no high or low."
Naturally it forms the seven treasures, gathering them across into all things; the light, essence, and brightness all emerge together, excellent and good beyond all compare: this means that
all things flow forth naturally from the one great treasury of light,
with subtle light shining forth in splendor,
beyond all compare.
Master Hanshan says:
"When you see the place where not a single thought arises
(utterly true and utterly white)
, then the former and latter limits are cut off, and the middle stands alone. Suddenly the lacquer bucket is smashed, and in an instant you see your original face
(understanding the mind and seeing the nature)
. Then body, mind, and world all at once sink away, like the shadows of flowers in the sky falling
(the illusory shadows of sky-flowers cease)
, and the ten directions are perfectly bright, forming one great treasury of light."
(Dream Roaming Collection
Pointing Out the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation and Chan Contemplation.)
Former and latter limits: the former limit is the past, the latter limit the future. The Jingying Commentary says:
Conditioned dharmas arise one after another, front and back. The front is the former limit, the back the latter limit."

The former and latter limits cut off, and the middle stands alone: with no former thought and no latter thought, a state of luminous, vividly clear awareness standing alone — that is, the state in which not a single thought arises. The Record of the Mirror of the Source:
If not a single thought arises, then the former and latter limits are cut off. The illuminating essence stands independent; thing and self are both suchness, directly reaching the source of mind."
The Prefaces to the Collected Explanations of the Sources of Chan says:
Hearing once, one awakens to a thousand things and gains the great dharanis; not a single thought arises, and the former and latter limits are cut off."
Sinking away: also written "sinking away" — to vanish.
The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure Equality and Enlightenment (Han translation) says:

"Once one opens through to clarity, the natural within the natural shows its natural aspect, and the natural has its root. Naturally it forms five lights up to nine colors, and the five lights up to nine colors wheel and turn, with hundreds and thousands of further transformations — the most supreme naturalness. Naturally it forms the seven treasures, gathering them across into all things; the light and essence wheel and shine forth together, excellent and fair beyond all limit."
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:
"It abides in neither above nor below, penetrating without limit."
The next passage again exhorts us toward birth in the Pure Land. This is the World-Honored One's endlessly repeated exhortation, born of inexhaustible compassion.

Each of you should diligently strive and seek earnestly for yourselves. You will surely transcend and pass beyond, to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Cutting across the five destinies, the evil paths close of themselves. The supreme Way of the Infinite, easy to go to yet with none who go; that land turns none away, and only naturalness pulls beings along. Cast aside your aims like empty space, and diligently practice in quest of the Way and its virtue. You may attain the utmost longevity, with life and bliss beyond all limit. Why cling to worldly affairs and fret
náo
and worry over impermanence?

Since the Land of Ultimate Bliss is so excellent, each of you should strive with diligence and seek birth there for yourselves. You will surely transcend the three realms, be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and leave the six paths of cyclic existence behind. This incomparable golden highway of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is easy to go to yet with none who go; the Land of Ultimate Bliss turns no one away. Those beings who are not born there are drawn along naturally by their own deathbed delusions, and so take birth in the six paths. Therefore you must certainly let go of all conditions, making your mind like empty space (cast aside your aims like empty space), and diligently practice the Pure Land Dharma-gate. Once born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, you attain eternal life, with longevity and bliss beyond all limit. Why then cling to worldly affairs and anxiously dread the coming of death (impermanence)?
The evil paths close of themselves: the evil paths here are
the "five evil paths" spoken of in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation): hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

"Each of you should diligently strive and seek earnestly for yourselves. You will surely transcend and pass beyond, to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Cutting across the five evil paths, the paths of destiny close of themselves. Rising on the Way without end or limit, easy to go to yet with none who go; that land turns none away, and only naturalness pulls beings along. Why not cast aside worldly affairs and diligently practice in quest of the Way and its virtue? You may attain the utmost longevity, with life and bliss beyond all limit."

The five evil paths: namely, hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. Because these five paths are the roads of birth-and-death and cyclic existence, for a cultivator who would end birth and death and leave the three realms, they are all evil paths.

Easy to go to yet with none who go: the phrase "easy to go to" here is spoken in relation to other Dharma-gates. In the Chan school, for instance, one must pass through the ten thousand thoughts returning to one (which corresponds to the Pure Land school's single-mindedness), then one returning to nothing, then understanding the mind and seeing the nature; and afterward one must keep up the work of preservation, cutting off afflictions, before one can end birth and death and leave cyclic existence. The Pure Land Dharma-gate, by contrast, requires only ten continuous recitations at the end of life to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and so end birth and death and leave cyclic existence. Hence it is called
"easy to go to."
The Jiayang Commentary says:
"Simply accomplish ten recitations
(accomplish ten continuous recitations at the end of life)
, and one attains birth, yet those who practice so are rare
(yet those who earnestly do so are very few).
Therefore it is said, 'easy to go to yet with none who go.'"
That land turns none away, and only naturalness pulls beings along: the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:
"That land turns none away
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss refuses no sentient being who would be born there)
, and only naturalness pulls them along
(those beings who are not born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are drawn naturally by their own deathbed delusions to take birth in the six paths)."
The six paths: hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and gods. The Way and its virtue: the true Dharma is called the Way; to attain the Way and not lose it is called virtue. Fret (
náo)
and worry: the appearance of a heart troubled by fear.

Those beings who are not born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are drawn naturally by their own deathbed delusions to take birth in the six paths: on this point Master Lianchi, in his Commentary and Notes on the Amitabha Sutra, teaches:
One whose mind is inverted at the end of life
has, through following deluded thoughts day after day and failing to cultivate right mindfulness, a mind full of distraction. At the moment when warmth and touch are about to be relinquished
(when the four elements break apart)

, everything one has done in life appears before one; the mind and spirit are terrified, and one's movements and bearing are frantic. One who is destined for hell sees knife-mountains and sword-trees as pleasure gardens. One who is destined for animal rebirth takes the mare's womb and the donkey's womb for a hall of state. Even one who has done good and is bound for the human or heavenly realms cannot escape hating or loving his parents. Even the early sages, in the first stage of the Lesser Vehicle, and bodhisattvas who have just brought forth the resolve, are still unable to know their entering and departing rightly. All of this is what is called inversion. Carried along by this inversion, one receives birth throughout the three realms and seven destinies according to one's karma.

As the Buddha said: 'When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.' He also said: 'All lands are upheld by mind alone.' When the contemplation of purity is accomplished, one is certain to attain rebirth. Of this there is no doubt whatsoever."
(For further teachings, see
Right Mindfulness at the End of Life

Translation: One whose mind is inverted at the end of life is inverted because, through following deluded thoughts day after day and failing to cultivate right mindfulness, the mind is full of distraction. When the four elements break apart, everything done in life appears before one; the mind and spirit are terrified and one's bearing is frantic. One destined for hell takes the knife-mountains and sword-trees for beautiful pleasure gardens. One destined for animal rebirth takes the mare's womb and the donkey's womb for splendid halls. Even one who has done good and should be born in the human or heavenly realms cannot, at the moment of entering the womb, escape loving the mother and hating the father, and so takes a male body, or loving the father and hating the mother, and so takes a female body. Even the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle and the bodhisattva who has just brought forth the resolve still suffer the delusion of passing through the womb, and cannot know their entering and departing rightly. All of this is inversion. Because of the inversion at the end of life, one receives birth throughout the seven destinies within the three realms according to one's karma.

As the Buddha said: 'When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.' (When one's own mind is pure, the Buddha-land in which one is born is pure as well.) The Buddha also said: 'All lands are upheld by mind alone.' (
All lands exist solely in dependence on the mind's thoughts. As it is said, 'When the mind arises, all dharmas arise.'

) Therefore, when the practitioner of Buddha-recitation accomplishes the contemplation of purity, that person is certain to attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Of this, of course, there is not the slightest doubt.

The seven destinies: hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, immortals, gods, and asuras. "Destiny" means the direction toward which one tends. Buddha-land: the territory taught and transformed by one Buddha; it is divided into pure lands, impure lands, reward lands, and the land of the Dharma-nature.

blocks.text: 4. Rejoicing in and Seeking the Pure Land, Renouncing and Leaving the Saha World

inline.s: Rejoicing in and seeking, renouncing and leaving: to rejoice in and seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and to renounce and leave the Saha World. The sufferings of the Saha World are too bitter for words; the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is beyond all metaphor. (See
Rejoicing in the Pure Land, Renouncing the Saha World
for details.)
Exhortation: to admonish and make clear. Encouragement: to urge one onward.

People of the world all contend over matters that need not be rushed, and amid this fierce evil and bitter suffering they labor body and mind to provide for themselves. High and low, rich and poor, young and old, men and women, all pile up thoughts and brood over plans, driven about by their minds. Those without fields worry about fields; those without houses worry about houses; for relatives and wealth, those who have and those who lack alike worry.

People of the world all contend over trivial matters that need not be rushed; amid this fierce evil and bitter suffering they labor and manage, to provide for themselves. High and low, rich and poor, young and old, men and women all pile up thoughts and brood over schemes, driven by their deluded minds. Those without fields worry about fields; those without houses worry about houses; and as for relatives and possessions, those who have them and those who lack them all worry alike (those who lack them long to have them; those who have them fear to lose them, and long for even more).

Matters that need not be rushed: to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, to end birth and death and escape cyclic existence — this is the most important matter of all in human life, and this alone is the urgent task. All worldly affairs are matters that need not be rushed. The people of the world all contend over matters that need not be rushed: people of the world all rush about contending over trivial affairs, and pay no heed to what is truly urgent for themselves. Not knowing how swiftly impermanence comes or how great the matter of birth and death is, they spend all their energy and time on worldly affairs. Greedy only for fame and profit, beset by a myriad cares and sorrows, the result is that they find no end to cyclic existence in the six paths.
Practitioners of Buddha-recitation all know that
"contending over matters that need not be rushed"
is delusion, yet those who can truly savor its meaning and act upon it are few. The remedy is:
habituation.

Habituation is wisdom permeating delusion: the element of wisdom gradually increases while the element of delusion gradually decreases. When wisdom becomes the master, one can decide for oneself where to go and what to do (previously it was karmic power that decided), and the obstacles in one's study and practice are resolved as they arise. Therefore habituation is an extremely important part of study and practice.

Time passes swiftly and human life is impermanent. Practitioners of Buddha-recitation must be ever vigilant, and must never take things lightly, squandering their time until their regret is endless. The bodhisattva Samantabhadra says in his Verse to Awaken the Multitude:
"This day has passed, and with it our lives have diminished. Like fish in dwindling water, what
(what)
joy can there be? Great assembly: strive with diligence, as though your hair were on fire! Only think on impermanence
(only think on the coming of death)
, and do not be heedless
(never give way to indulgence and pleasure)
A fish in dwindling water: a fish in a pond whose waters daily run dry.
Strive with diligence, as though your hair were on fire:
a great fire is blazing on your head, and death is closing in swiftly. The practitioner of Buddha-recitation should
strive with unflagging diligence,
and quickly
without a moment's delay, before coma and death overtake him, accomplish the ten continuous recitations until they become second nature (for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth

). Impermanence: the absence of permanence (all things in the world arise and cease, shifting and flowing, never abiding for even an instant); it also refers to death, and to the ghost that claims the soul. Do not be heedless: never give way to indulgence and pleasure so as to waste body, mind, and time. The Buddha says:
"Though for one lifetime you strive and suffer, in but a moment you will be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss beyond all limit."
(The Sutra of Immeasurable Life, Han translation)

Having one thing, they lack another, and their thoughts long to be equal. When they have just a little, they worry again about the unusual. Water, fire, thieves, enemies, and creditors flood and burn them, rob and seize them, scatter and destroy them. Their minds are stingy and their wills stubborn, and they cannot let go. At the end of life all is abandoned, and not one thing follows them. Rich and poor alike are the same, with a myriad cares and sorrows.

Having gained one thing, they feel they still lack another, and compare themselves endlessly (their thoughts long to be equal); the gully of desire is hard to fill. When they have just a little, they worry that it cannot last, and that everything they possess will be flooded, burned, robbed, trampled, or plundered by water, fire, thieves, enemies (including wastrel sons), and creditors, and so scattered and destroyed. Their minds are stingy and stubborn, and they cannot let go. Yet at the end of life they must finally part with it all, and not one thing can be carried away. Rich and poor are alike in this, with a myriad cares and sorrows.

At the end of life all is abandoned, and not one thing follows them: ten thousand things cannot be taken along; only karma follows the body. Once impermanence arrives, then you will know you were a person in a dream.

People of the world, fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, relatives and kin, should mutually respect and love one another, and not hate or envy one another. They should share what they have and supply what others lack, and must not be greedy or stingy. Their words and looks should always be harmonious, and they should not oppose or demean one another. If at times their minds contend and anger and resentment arise, in later lives it becomes ever worse, until it grows into great enmity. Worldly affairs bring mutual harm; though it does not come upon them at once, one should urgently reflect and break through it.

People of the world, fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, relatives and kin, should mutually respect and love one another, and should not hate or envy one another. They should help one another and share what they have, and must not be greedy or stingy. They should speak with kind words and loving speech, and should not oppose or mock one another. If for a time there is opposition and a contending mind arises, with hatred and strife, then in later lives it grows worse by turns, until it becomes great enmity (these four sentences mean that in the world, often a small matter is not endured, and so it grows into great enmity and deep hatred, even to the destruction of the family and the loss of life). Worldly affairs bring mutual harm; though the evil fruit does not appear at the time (though it does not come at once), the evil cause has already been made, and where there is a cause there will be an effect. One should at once reflect and break through these causal relations, and not act rashly (these sentences mean that one should be a clear-headed person regarding cause and effect. Sentient beings only know to fear the fruit; bodhisattvas know to fear the cause).

Amid craving and desire, people are alone in birth and alone in death, alone in going and alone in coming; suffering and joy they bear themselves, and none can take their place. Good and evil change, and each pursues where it is born; their roads differ, and the time of meeting is without limit. Why not, while strong and well, strive to cultivate goodness? What are you waiting for?

People are sunk in love and desire, and do not understand that in truth they are alone in birth and alone in death, alone in going and alone in coming, bearing their own suffering and joy, with none to take their place. Each person's good and evil change; fruit follows the cause that gives rise to it, and since causes and effects differ, their roads after death also differ, and the time of meeting is without limit. Why not, while strong and well, strive to cultivate goodness? What are you waiting for?

People of the world cannot see their own good and evil, and so they race one another to do what brings fortune or misfortune, calamity or blessing. Body foolish and spirit dark, they turn to take up other teachings, and inversion continues unbroken, the root of impermanence. Blind and obdurate, they do not believe in the sutras and Dharma. Their minds have no far-reaching concern; each wishes only for present pleasure. Deluded by anger and greed, they covet wealth and beauty. They never cease, and pitiful and grievous it is!

People of the world are deluded, unable to see their own good and evil, and do not understand the causes and effects of fortune and misfortune, calamity and blessing. They seek only the pleasure of the moment, and race one another to act (not knowing the cause, they do not fear the fruit). Body foolish and spirit dark (deeds stupid, mind benighted); such inverted views are then taught from one to another (one need only look at today's films, news, and literature, full of killing, stealing, and lust and of greed, anger, and delusion, soaking children, young people, and adults alike through the eyes and ears, to know how "inverted views are taught from one to another"); inverted and contrary conduct continues unbroken, and this is the root of birth-and-death and cyclic existence. Blind and obdurate (childish and ignorant of reason), they oppose and defy, and do not believe in the sutras and Dharma. Their minds have no far-reaching concern; each seeks only the pleasure of the moment. Deluded by anger and greed, they covet wealth and beauty. They never cease, and pitiful and grievous it is!

Their forebears were not good, and did not know morality, and there was no one to tell them; small wonder it is. The destinies of death and birth, the paths of good and evil, they do not believe in at all, and say there is no such thing. Let them look at one another, and they will see it for themselves.

Their forebears were not good (both foolish and wicked), and did not know morality, so no one came to teach them rightly; hence their deeds are stupid and their minds benighted, and there is nothing strange in it. The destinies toward which death and birth tend, the six paths of good and evil, they do not believe in at all, and say there is no such thing. Yet one need only observe carefully, and one will see it for oneself.

Sometimes a father weeps for a son, sometimes a son weeps for a father; brothers, husbands and wives weep for one another in turn. One dies, one lives, and each looks back with longing. Care and love bind them, and there is no time of release. Their thoughts dwell on kindness and affection, and they never part from craving and desire. They cannot think deeply and plan carefully, or devote themselves single-mindedly to the Way. Their years and lifespan swiftly end, and there is nothing to be done!

Sometimes the son dies and the father weeps, sometimes the father dies and the son weeps; brothers, husbands and wives weep for one another. One dies, one lives, and they cannot bear to part. Care and love bind them, and there is no time of release. They think always of kindness, love, and delight, and never part from craving and desire. Yet they cannot think deeply and plan carefully, or devote themselves single-mindedly to the Way. Their lifespan ends in an instant, and there is nothing to be done!
In turn: one after another.

Those deluded about the Way are many; those who awaken to the Way are few. Each harbors the poison of killing, and evil airs hang dark. For delusion they stir up affairs, opposing heaven and earth. Giving free rein to their crimes until they reach the extreme, their lifespan is suddenly taken away. They descend into the evil paths, with no time of escape.

Those deluded about the Way are many; those who awaken to the Way are few. Each harbors a mind of killing (destroying the other) and poison (malice), and evil airs spread everywhere. They stir up affairs and do evil, opposing heaven and earth. Giving free rein to their crimes until they reach the extreme (their evil is full to overflowing), their lifespan is suddenly taken away, and they descend into the evil paths, with no time of escape.

You should think deeply and plan carefully, keep far from all evil, choose what is good, and diligently practice it. Craving, desire, glory, and splendor cannot be kept forever; all must be parted from, and there is nothing to delight in. You should strive with diligence and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. There wisdom is clear and penetrating, and merit and virtue are supreme. Do not follow your own desires, fail the sutras and precepts, and fall behind others.

You should think deeply and plan carefully, keep far from all evil, choose what is good, and diligently practice it. Craving, desire, glory, and splendor cannot be kept forever; all must be parted from, and there is nothing to delight in. You should strive with diligence and seek birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once there, wisdom is clear and penetrating, and merit and virtue are supreme. You must never follow your own desires, fail the sutras and precepts, and fall behind others.

You: all of you. Strive with diligence and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss: though for one lifetime you strive with diligence and suffer hardship, it is but a moment; afterward you are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss beyond all limit.

Maitreya said: The Buddha's words of teaching and admonition are profound and excellent. We have all received your compassionate grace and are freed from care and suffering. The Buddha is the king of Dharma, honored above all sages; his light shines everywhere, penetrating without limit, and he is the teacher of all gods and humans. Now that we have met the Buddha and again heard the name of Immeasurable Life, there is none who is not joyful, and our minds attain clarity.

The bodhisattva Maitreya said to the World-Honored One: The Buddha's words of teaching and admonition are profound and excellent. We have all received the Buddha's compassionate grace and are freed from care and suffering. The Buddha is the king of Dharma, honored above all sages; his light shines everywhere, penetrating without limit, and he is the teacher of all gods and humans. Today we have received the Buddha's teaching and admonition, and we have again heard the name of Amitabha Buddha (how important this is! If one does not even know the name of Amitabha Buddha, how could one be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and end birth and death and escape cyclic existence?). There is none who is not joyful, and our minds attain clarity.

The Buddha told Maitreya: To revere the Buddha is to be greatly good. You should truly recite the Buddha's name, cut off the fox's doubt, uproot all craving and desire, and block up the sources of all evil. Then you may walk throughout the three realms without obstruction, reveal the right Way, and save those not yet saved.

The Buddha told the bodhisattva Maitreya: To revere the Buddha is to be greatly good. You should truly recite the Buddha's name, cut off the fox's doubt, uproot all craving and desire, and block up (stop up) the sources of all evil. When you are born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, you may then walk throughout the three realms without obstruction, reveal the right Way, and save those not yet saved.

Truly recite the Buddha's name, cut off the fox's doubt: the fox is by nature full of doubt, and so uncertain doubt is called "the fox's doubt." The fundamental reason practitioners fear difficulty and grow indolent is that they half-believe and half-doubt the Pure Land sutras and treatises and the teachings of the patriarchs (believing some and doubting some, or believing for a while and then doubting again). If one's faith is true and one's vow is keen, one will certainly follow the sutras, treatises, and the patriarchs' teachings, practice exactly as taught, and press bravely forward:
thoughts continuing in unbroken succession, with the end of life as the limit, steeling the mind and mastering oneself, never ceasing day or night
(for details see
Master Shandao's Three Teachings
—This is the path of "ten out of ten will be born, a hundred out of a hundred will be born" revealed to us by Master Shandao, who was Amitabha Buddha come again.

You should know that the people of the ten directions, from kalpas without beginning, have turned and turned through the six paths, with care and suffering unbroken. At birth there is suffering, in old age there is suffering, in grave illness there is suffering, and in death there is extreme suffering. Foul and impure, there is nothing to delight in. You should resolve for yourselves, wash away the stains of the mind, and let your words and deeds be loyal and true, with the outer and the inner corresponding.

You should know that the people of the ten directions, since kalpas without beginning, have all turned and turned in cyclic existence through the six paths, with care and suffering unbroken. At birth there is suffering, in old age there is suffering, in grave illness there is suffering, and in death there is extreme suffering. Foul and impure, there is nothing to delight in. You should resolve firmly, cut off the causes of evil, wash away the stains of the mind, and let your words and deeds be loyal and true, with the outer and the inner corresponding.
People can save themselves, and then save one another in turn. With sincere hearts they seek their vow, and accumulate the roots of goodness.
Though for one lifetime you strive and suffer, in but a moment you will be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss beyond all limit.
Forever uprooting the root of birth and death, free of the affliction of care and suffering, with life of a thousand million kalpas, at ease and as you wish.

Only when people can save themselves can they save others; thus in turn they rescue one another. You should with sincere hearts vow to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and accumulate the roots of goodness. Though for one lifetime you strive with diligence and suffer hardship, it is but a moment; afterward you are born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, with bliss beyond all limit. Forever uprooting the root of birth and death, no longer afflicted by care and suffering, with a lifespan of a thousand million kalpas, at ease and as you wish.

The roots of goodness: roots of virtue and goodness. Because goodness is the cause of bodhi, it is called a root of goodness, a root of good. To accumulate the roots of goodness: this means single-mindedly reciting Amitabha Buddha's name. Because holding the name in recitation is precisely the root of goodness for rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, to accumulate the roots of goodness here means to single-mindedly recite Amitabha Buddha's name.
Each should strive diligently and seek what his heart desires. Do not doubt or regret, bringing fault upon yourselves
(jiù)
, and be born in the borderland, in the city of seven treasures, where for five hundred years you will undergo every hardship.

You must each strive diligently, seek what your hearts desire, and be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Do not doubt or regret, bringing fault upon yourselves, and be born in the borderland, in the city of seven treasures, where for five hundred years you will undergo every hardship.
Fault (jiù): transgression; error. The borderland and the city of seven treasures: for details see "40. The Doubting City in the Borderland" below.
Maitreya said: Having received the Buddha's clear teaching, we will single-mindedly and diligently study and practice, follow the teaching in practice, and dare not doubt.

The bodhisattva Maitreya said to the World-Honored One: Having received the Buddha's wise and clear teaching, we will certainly single-mindedly and diligently study, follow the teaching in practice, and dare not doubt.

blocks.text: 35. The Evil Suffering of the Turbid World

inline.s: The turbid world: the evil world of the five turbidities. This world has five turbidities: the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of lifespan. Hence it is called the evil world of the five turbidities, or the turbid world for short.
The Buddha Speaks the Amitabha Sutra says:

"Shariputra! As I now praise the inconceivable merits of all Buddhas, those Buddhas likewise praise my inconceivable merits, saying: Śākyamuni Buddha is able to accomplish what is most difficult and rare! In the Saha World, in the evil world of the five turbidities (the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of lifespan), he attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and, for the sake of all sentient beings, taught this Dharma that is hard for the world to believe."

The turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of lifespan: the turbidity of the kalpa means being born in the final age, when war, famine, and plague arise one after another, and living beings are plunged into misery with never a day of peace. The turbidity of views means that people of the world hold wrong views, do not follow the right Way, and are lost in a welter of differing teachings with no consensus. The turbidity of afflictions means that people of the world are full of craving, anger, contention, and unending deceit. The turbidity of sentient beings means that people of the world are mostly corrupt and evil, impure in body (conduct) and mind, and do not penetrate the meaning of the truth. The turbidity of lifespan means that sentient beings, their afflictions crowding upon them and body and mind worn out, have short lifespans.

The evil suffering of the turbid world: evil is the cause, suffering the fruit. The evil of the turbid world is the five evils; the suffering of the turbid world is the five pains and the five burnings. The five evils are the karmic cause; the five pains and five burnings are the karmic retribution. Within that retribution: the five pains are the flower retribution, and the five burnings are the fruit retribution.

The Buddha told Maitreya: If you can, in this world, rectify your minds and set your thoughts right, and do no evil, you are of great virtue. Why is that? In the worlds of the ten directions, good is much and evil is little, and they are easy to teach and transform. Only this world of the five evils is the most bitterly suffering. I now become a Buddha here, teaching and transforming the multitudes, causing them to forsake the five evils, put away the five pains, and leave the five burnings, subduing and transforming their minds, causing them to hold the five goods and obtain their merit and blessing.

The Buddha told the bodhisattva Maitreya: If you can, in this world, rectify your minds and set your thoughts right, and do no evil, you are of great virtue. Why is that? In the worlds of the ten directions, good is much and evil is little, and they are easy to teach and transform. Only this world of the five evils is the most bitterly suffering. I now become a Buddha here, teaching and transforming sentient beings, causing them to forsake the five evils, put away the five pains, and leave the five burnings, subduing and transforming their will to do evil, causing them to hold the five goods and obtain merit and blessing.

The five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking alcohol — these are the five evils. Those who commit these five evils, in this present life, are like criminals punished by the law, suffering misfortune in body; this is called the five pains. Because of these five evils, in future lives they fall into the three evil paths and receive retribution; this is called the five burnings. The five evils are the karmic cause; the five pains and the five burnings are the karmic retribution. Within that retribution: the five pains are the flower retribution, and the five burnings are the fruit retribution. The karmic cause: the cause of retribution for good and evil. Good karma is the cause of joyful fruit, evil karma the cause of bitter fruit. The flower retribution: also written "flower retribution." The flower opens before the fruit is formed, so "flower retribution" is spoken in contrast to the "fruit retribution" obtained afterward. For instance, one plants a tree to obtain its fruit; besides obtaining the fruit itself, one also obtains flowers — this is the flower retribution. When sentient beings plant the karmic causes of good and evil, the fruit obtained directly from those causes is the fruit retribution, and what is obtained along the way before the fruit retribution is called the flower retribution. The five goods: the five precepts — not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol.
Not drinking alcohol: not drinking or ingesting alcoholic beverages or drugs that intoxicate human nature.

Merit and blessing: the reward of blessing produced by cultivating the good deeds of humans and gods. Merit and blessing differ from merit and virtue: outward cultivation of worldly works, which is defiled good, is "merit and blessing"; inward realization of the Buddha-nature, which is undefiled good, is "merit and virtue." Again, cultivating the Way while clinging to marks is "merit and blessing"; cultivating the Way free of marks is "merit and virtue." Hence in bodhisattva practice "no marks" is often mentioned, and no marks means to be free of marks while amidst marks. (For details see
The Three No's: No Thought, No Marks, No Dwelling
) The defiled: defilement is another name for affliction; to be defiled is to have afflictions, and to be undefiled is to be free of afflictions.

What are the five? The first: among the living beings of the world, some wish to do every evil. The strong overpower the weak and turn on one another with plunder and harm, maiming and killing, devouring one another in turn
(dàn).
Not knowing to do good, afterward they receive calamity and punishment. Hence there are the poor and beggars, the lonely and orphaned, the deaf and blind
, the mute
(yīn,
unable to speak
and dumb
, the stupid and wicked, the hunchbacked
wāng

and insane. All this is because in former lives they did not believe in morality and would not do good. Those who are noble and wealthy, wise elders, brave and talented, all owe it to compassion and filial piety in former lives, to cultivating goodness and accumulating virtue.

What are the five? The first: among the living beings of the world, some wish to do every evil. The strong oppress the weak and turn on one another with plunder and harm (plunder and harm), maiming and killing, devouring one another in turn. Not knowing to do good, afterward they receive calamity and punishment. Hence there are the poor and beggars, the orphaned and widowed, the deaf and blind, the mute and foolish, the crippled and insane. All this is because in former lives they did not believe in morality and would not do good. And those who are noble and wealthy, wise elders, brave and talented, all owe it to compassion, loyalty, and filial piety in former lives, to cultivating goodness and accumulating virtue.
The widowed (guān) and the solitary: widowers (men without wives) and widows. The hunchbacked (wāng): the bones bent and crooked out of shape; it also refers to those with such a disability.

In this world such things exist, plainly before our eyes. After the end of life, one enters the dark realm, is reborn and receives a body, changes form and alters course. Hence there are hell-beings, birds and beasts, and the fliers and wrigglers. It is like the prisons of worldly law, with bitter torture and extreme punishment; the soul, spirit, and vital essence follow their crimes
(here meaning "tend")

toward their destination. The lifespan they receive, whether long or short, they are born together and repay one another in turn. Until their evil is exhausted they can never leave. They turn and turn within it, and for many kalpas find no escape. Deliverance is hard to gain, and the pain is beyond words. Between heaven and earth this is naturally so. Though retribution does not strike at once, good and evil will surely come home to them.

Those who commit such evil receive these present retributions in this life. After their death they come to the dark realm, are reborn and receive a body, change form (casting off the human body) and alter course (falling into the evil paths). Hence there are hells (niraya), birds and beasts, and the fliers and wrigglers. It is like the prisons of worldly law, with bitter torture and extreme punishment: the consciousness (soul, spirit, and vital essence) is punished according to the size of its crimes. The lifespan they receive, whether long or short — enemy and foe are born together and repay one another in turn (enmity repaid with enmity, without end). Until their evil is exhausted they can never leave the evil paths. They turn and turn within it, and for many kalpas find no escape. Deliverance is hard to gain, and the pain is beyond words. Between heaven and earth this law of cause and effect is natural. Even if retribution does not strike at once and violently, the retribution of good and evil will finally be fulfilled.

Niraya: a transliteration of the Sanskrit; it means hell. It is like the prisons of worldly law, with bitter torture and extreme punishment: it is like worldly law punishing criminals, first shutting them in prison with the body in chains, tortured and interrogated — this illustrates the flower retribution in this present body; and at the last they are put to extreme punishment and their lives cut off — this illustrates the fruit retribution after death.

Second: the people of the world do not follow the laws and rules, but are extravagant, licentious, arrogant, and unrestrained, following their own minds at will. Those above are not enlightened, those in office are not upright; they entrap the innocent and harm the loyal and good. Their minds and mouths differ, and their scheming and falsity are manifold. High and low, kin and stranger, deceive one another. Angry and deluded, they wish to enrich themselves and covet much. In profit and loss, victory and defeat, they knot up resentment and become enemies, ruin their families and lose their lives, heedless of what comes before and after. Though rich, they are stingy and will not give. Their love clings and their greed is heavy; their minds toil and their bodies suffer. Thus to the very end, not one thing follows them. Good and evil, misfortune and blessing, pursue where their lives are born; some are born in pleasant places, others enter bitter poison.

Second: the people of the world do not follow the laws and rules, but are extravagant, licentious, arrogant, and unrestrained, following their own minds at will and seeking only their own pleasure. Those above are not enlightened, those in office are not upright; they entrap the innocent and harm the loyal and good. Their minds and mouths differ (with benevolence and righteousness on the lips and killing, stealing, lust, and falsehood in the heart), and their scheming and falsity are manifold; whether high or low, kin or stranger, they deceive them all. Angry and deluded, they wish to enrich themselves (desiring only their own advantage) and covet much (desiring only to have more and more). In deceit and contention, in profit and loss, victory and defeat, they knot up resentment and become enemies, ruin their families and lose their lives, heedless of what comes before and after. Though rich, they are stingy by nature and will not give. Their craving is firm and their greed deep; their minds toil and their bodies suffer. Thus at the end of life, not one thing follows them (they cannot take a single thing along). The blessing of good causes and the calamity of evil causes follow the world into which they are born. Some are born in pleasant places, others enter bitter poison.
Again, some see goodness and hate and slander it, and do not think to admire and follow it. They always harbor a thieving mind, hope
xī

for others' profit and use it to supply themselves, and when they have squandered it they take again. The gods mark it all, and in the end they enter the evil paths. Of themselves there are the three paths, with immeasurable affliction, in which they turn and turn, and for many kalpas find no escape, with pain beyond words.

Again, some see goodness and hate and slander it, and do not think to admire and follow it. They always harbor a thieving mind, scheming for others' profit and using it to supply themselves, and when they have squandered it they take again. The gods record it all, and at the end of life they enter the evil paths. Of themselves there are the three paths
(the three evil paths)
with immeasurable affliction, in which they turn and turn, and for many kalpas find no escape, with pain beyond words.

Hope (xī): to long for. Marking it all: to record without the slightest omission. To mark is to record; all means without omission. The gods mark it all: the good and evil of a person are recorded by the gods without the slightest omission.
Good and evil will be repaid in the end; three feet above your head are the gods.
Third: the people of the world, born one from another, how long is their lifespan? The unwholesome, in body and mind unright, always harbor evil and constantly think lewd
yì
thoughts. Their breasts are full of turmoil and their lewd bearing shows outwardly. They waste the family wealth and do what is unlawful. What they ought to seek, they refuse to do.

Third: the people of the world, born one from another (all are born here by the karmic causes they have made), how long is their lifespan (how long can they live)? The unwholesome, in body and mind unright, always harbor evil and are lewd and dissolute. Their breasts are full of turmoil and their lewd bearing shows outwardly. (The deeds of lust) waste the family wealth and are unlawful. What they ought to seek, they refuse to do.
Lewd (
yì
): dissolute.

Again, some form factions and gather together, raise troops and attack one another. They assault, rob, and slaughter, seize by force and coerce, and give what they take to wife and children, indulging their bodies in pleasure. All alike hate and loathe them, and suffer and are pained by them. Such evil as this is known to humans and ghosts. The gods record it, and they fall of themselves into the three paths. With immeasurable affliction they turn and turn within them, and for many kalpas find no escape, with pain beyond words.

Again, some form factions and gather together, raise troops and attack one another. They assault, rob, and slaughter, seize by force and threaten, and give (the goods they rob and plunder) to wife and children, indulging in pleasure to the full. All alike hate and loathe them, and suffer and are pained by them. Such evil as this is known to humans and ghosts. The gods record it, and they fall of themselves into the three paths (the three evil paths). With immeasurable affliction they turn and turn within them, and for many kalpas find no escape, with pain beyond words.

Fourth: the people of the world do not think to cultivate goodness. With divisive speech and harsh words, falsehood and frivolous talk, they hate and envy good people and ruin the worthy and wise. They are unfilial to their parents and slight their teachers and elders. Toward friends they have no trust, and are rarely honest. Proud and arrogant, they claim to have the Way. They run amok with power and might, and oppress others. They wish others to fear and respect them, and feel no shame or fear themselves. They always harbor arrogance and pride, and are hard to subdue and transform.

Fourth: the people of the world do not think to cultivate goodness. With divisive speech and harsh words, falsehood and frivolous talk, they hate and envy good people and attack and slander the worthy and wise. They are unfilial to their parents and slight their teachers and elders. Toward friends they have no trust and are rarely honest. Proud and arrogant, they claim to have the Way. They run amok and tyrannize, oppressing others by their power. They wish others to fear and respect them, and feel no shame, fear, or remorse themselves. Their minds always harbor arrogance and tyranny, and they are hard to teach and subdue.

Relying on the merit and blessing of former lives that guarded and protected them, in this life they do evil, and their merit and blessing are utterly destroyed. When their lifespan ends, all evils gather around them. Moreover their names are recorded by the gods. Their guilt draws them on, and there is no way to leave it. They can only go forward, entering the fire-cauldron
huò
. Body and mind are shattered, and spirit and form suffer to the extreme. At such a time, what use is regret?

That one is a human being in this life is owing to the merit and blessing of former lives that guarded and protected one; but if one does evil in this life, one's merit and blessing are utterly destroyed. When one's lifespan ends, all evils gather around one. Moreover one's name and all one's deeds are recorded one by one by the gods. Once life ends, guilt (evil karma) draws one on, and there is no way to leave the evil paths. The consciousness can only go forward, entering the furnace fire and boiling cauldron of hell. Body and mind are shattered, and spirit and form suffer to the extreme. At such a time, regret comes too late!
Cauldron (
huò
): a great pot, often used as an instrument of execution for boiling people. The boiling cauldron: the cruel punishment of casting a person into a pot of boiling water to be boiled to death.

Fifth: the people of the world loiter and laze, unwilling to do good or to govern body and cultivate their work. To their parents' teachings they are contrary and rebellious. They are like enemies; better to have no children at all. They betray grace and violate righteousness, and make no repayment. They give free rein to wandering and dissipation, steeped in wine and addicted to delicacies. Rude and overbearing
hù

, they oppose and defy, and do not know human feeling. Without righteousness or propriety, they cannot be admonished or made to understand. For the resources of their six kinds of kin and dependents, whether they have or lack, they feel no concern.

Fifth: the people of the world loiter and laze (loitering about), are indolent and lazy, unwilling to do good, unwilling to govern body and mind and cultivate right work. To their parents' teachings they are contrary (rebellious) and defiant, like enemies and foes — such children are better not to have. They betray grace and violate righteousness toward their parents, and make no repayment. They give free rein to wandering and dissipation, steeped in wine (drinking to excess) and addicted to delicacies (craving fine food). Rude (coarse) and overbearing (tyrannical), they oppose and defy (are contrary), and do not understand the way of being human (do not know human feeling). Without righteousness or propriety, they cannot be admonished (corrected) or made to understand (enlightened). As for the resources (the necessities that sustain life) of their six kinds of kin (father, mother, elder and younger brothers, wife, and children) and dependents, and whether these have or lack, they are utterly unconcerned.
Loitering about: to linger. Overbearing (
hù
): tyrannical and violent.

They do not think on the grace of their parents, nor keep the righteousness of teachers and friends. In thought, intention, body, and speech, there is not one good thing. They do not believe in the Buddhas' sutras and Dharma, nor in birth and death, good and evil. They wish to harm the true persons and to throw the assembly of monks into disorder. Deluded and benighted, they take themselves to be wise. They do not know whence they come at birth or where they go at death. Unbenevolent and unfilial, they hope for long life. Taught with compassionate hearts, they refuse to believe. Though spoken to with bitter words, it profits them nothing. Their minds are blocked and their understanding does not open. When the great command is about to end, regret and fear come together. They do not cultivate goodness beforehand, but only regret at the end. What use is regret afterward?

They do not think on the grace of their parents, nor keep in mind the righteousness of teachers and friends. In intention, thought, action, and speech, there is not one good thing (they have never done a single good deed). They do not believe in the Buddhas' sutras and Dharma, nor in birth and death and the retribution of good and evil. They wish to entrap true persons who have realized the fruit, and to throw the assembly of monks into disorder (to break the harmonious Sangha). Deluded and benighted, they take themselves to be wise. They do not know whence they come at birth or where they go at death. Unbenevolent and unfilial, they hope for long life. Taught with compassionate hearts, they refuse to believe. Though admonished with bitter words, it profits them nothing. Their minds are blocked and their understanding does not open. When the great command is about to end, regret and fear come together. They do not cultivate goodness beforehand, but only regret and fear at the end. What use is regret and fear then?

Between heaven and earth the six paths are clearly distinguished. The retribution of good and evil, calamity and blessing, support one another, and one bears it oneself; none can take one's place. The good person does good, passing from joy into joy, from light into light. The evil person does evil, passing from suffering into suffering, from darkness into darkness. Who can know this? Only the Buddha knows.

Between heaven and earth the six paths are clearly distinguished. The retribution of good and evil, calamity and blessing, follow one another, and one bears it all oneself; no one can take one's place. The good person does good, passing from joy into joy, from light into light. The evil person does evil, passing from suffering into suffering, from darkness into darkness. Who can know the reasons within? Only the Buddha knows.

Taught and revealed, yet those who believe and practice are few. Birth and death do not cease, and the evil paths do not end. People of the world such as these are hard to describe in full. Hence there are of themselves the three paths, with immeasurable affliction, in which they turn and turn. Life after life, kalpa after kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to gain, and the pain is beyond words.

The Buddha taught and revealed, yet those who believe and practice are few. Therefore their birth and death and cyclic existence do not cease, and their falling into the evil paths is unending. People of the world such as these are hard to speak of in full. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable affliction, in which they turn and turn. Life after life, kalpa after kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to gain, and the pain is beyond words.

Such are the five evils, five pains, and five burnings: they are like a great fire burning the human body. If one can, amid them, single-mindedly master the mind, rectify the body and set thoughts right, make words and deeds accord, and be utterly sincere in what one does; if one alone does all good and does no evil, then one's body alone is delivered, one obtains merit and blessing, and one may attain long life and the path of nirvana. This is the five great goods!

Such are the five evils, five pains, and five burnings: they are like a great fire burning the human body. If one can, amid them, single-mindedly master the mind (steeling the mind and mastering oneself), rectify the body and set thoughts right, make words and deeds accord, and be utterly sincere in what one does; if one alone does all good and does no evil, then one's body is delivered, one obtains merit and blessing, and one may attain long life and the path of nirvana. This is the five great goods!
(Xiangfu) matching; corresponding.
(Do good alone, commit no evil) The common precept verse of the Seven Buddhas says:
“Do no evil; practice every good; purify your own mind — this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
(This is the admonition of every Buddha).”
(The five great goods) Straighten body and mind, let words and deeds match each other, act with utmost sincerity, do good alone, and commit no evil.

[The Buddha told Maitreya: I tell you all, these five evils, five pains, and five burnings give rise to one another in turn. Those who dare to transgress them shall pass through the evil destinies. Perhaps in this present life they are first struck by sickness and calamity, unable to die and unable to live, shown to the multitude as a warning. Or at the end of life they enter the three evil paths, where sorrow, pain, and utter agony, and the hellfire of their own karma, burn (jiāo) them
jiāo
then
(anciently the same as “burn”)

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Maitreya: I tell you that these five evils, five pains, and five burnings give rise to one another in turn. Those who dare to transgress them shall pass through the evil paths. In this present life they first receive sickness and calamity (the flower retribution), unable to die and unable to live (unable to seek life and unable to seek death), so that the multitude may see them and know that cause and effect never fail. At the end of life they fall into the three evil paths (the fruit retribution), where sorrow, pain, and utter agony, and the hellfire of their own karma, consume them.
(Huo) means “there are.” (Kudu) means the most miserable of torments. (Zi xiang jiao (
jiāo
) ran
(anciently the same as “burn”)
) means that one's own karma brings the hellfire that burns one. The Huishu says:
“Jiao-ran describes the ferocity of the hellfire. Zi means that it is brought about by one's own karma.”

[With their enemies and foes they wound and kill one another again and again. From the smallest causes great disasters grow. All this comes of greedily clinging to wealth and lust, unwilling to give aid. Each seeks only his own pleasure, with no thought of right or wrong. Driven by deluded craving, they thicken self and contend for gain; riches and glory bring momentary delight. They cannot bear insult and do not strive to cultivate goodness. Their power lasts but a little while, then is wiped away. The way of heaven unfolds and of itself examines and exposes them; alone and afraid (
qióng
qióng song
sōng
song, they fall into it. This has been so in every age; how pitiful and grievous!]

With their enemies and foes they wound and kill one another without cease. From the smallest dispute great disasters grow. All this comes of greedily clinging to wealth and lust, unwilling to give aid. Each seeks only his own pleasure, with no thought of right or wrong. Driven by deluded craving, they thicken self and contend for gain; riches and glory bring momentary delight. They cannot bear insult and do not strive to cultivate goodness. Their power lasts but a little while, then is wiped away. The way of heaven unfolds, and of itself examines and exposes them (jiuju), and their own consciousness, alone and afraid (qiongqiong songsong), falls into the evil paths. This has been so in every age; how pitiful and grievous!
(Shizhang) means to carry out. (Qiong (
qióng
) qiong) means the appearance of being all alone. (Song (
sōng
) song) means the appearance of terror and unease.

[You have obtained the Buddha's words in the sutras; ponder them deeply and maturely, each of you keeping to them uprightly, never slackening to the end of your days. Honor the sages, respect the good, be kind and universally loving. Seek to cross beyond the world and pull out by the root the mass of evil that is birth and death. Depart from the three evil paths, that road of sorrow, terror, and pain.]

You are fortunate to have obtained the Buddha's teaching; you should ponder it again and again and deeply, each keeping to it uprightly and following it, never slackening to the end of your days. Honor the sages, respect the good, be kind and universally loving. Deliver yourself and deliver others, and pull out by the root the mass of evil that is birth and death. Depart from the three evil paths (hell, hungry ghosts, animals), that road of sorrow, terror, and pain.

[If you would do good, what comes first? You should make your own mind upright, make your own body upright; ear, eye, mouth, and nose should each be made upright. When body and mind are pure and clean, you accord with goodness. Do not follow your cravings; do not transgress against any evil. Let your words and countenance be harmonious, your bodily conduct single-minded. In every movement and every glance, be calm and composed, and act with deliberation. To act rashly and in haste brings failure and later regret. To do a thing without care loses all the merit of your effort.]

If you would do good, what comes first? It is to make your own mind upright, to make your own body upright; ear, eye, mouth, and nose should each be made upright. When body and mind are pure and clean, you accord with goodness. Do not follow your cravings and desires; do not transgress against any evil. Let your words and countenance be harmonious, your bodily conduct single-minded in the Way. In every movement and every glance, be calm and composed. To act rashly and in haste brings failure and later regret. To do a thing without care loses all the merit of your effort.

(Make your own mind upright, make your own body upright; ear, eye, mouth, and nose should each be made upright) Think nothing that is against principle, do nothing that is against principle, hear nothing that is against principle, see nothing that is against principle, say nothing that is against principle, smell nothing that is against principle.
(In every movement and every glance, be calm and composed) In every movement and every glance, be calm and composed.
(To act rashly and in haste) To act rashly and in haste without examining one's own thoughts and desires.

(Di) means careful. (To do a thing without care loses all the merit of your effort) Because one is not careful and prudent, one loses the merit of one's practice. Therefore, in whatever one undertakes, one should first carefully weigh what is right and what is harmful, and only act once it accords with principle; this is the awakened mind, and it is not the same as the wild and chaotic mind.

blocks.text: 37. Like the Poor Man Who Finds a Treasure

inline.s: [You should widely plant the roots of virtue and transgress against none of the precepts of the Way. Be patient and forbearing, diligent and vigorous, of compassionate mind and single-minded, pure in fasting and precepts. One day and one night here surpasses a hundred years of doing good in the Land of Immeasurable Life. Why is that? In that Buddha-land all beings accumulate virtue and every good, and there is not the least hair's-breadth of evil. If in this world one cultivates goodness for ten days and ten nights, the merit one gains surpasses a thousand years of doing good in the Buddha-lands of other directions. Why is that? In those Buddha-lands merit and virtue come of themselves, and there is no ground for creating evil. Only in this world is there little good and much evil; beings drink suffering and eat poison, and never for a moment find peace.]

You should widely plant the roots of virtue, and on no account transgress against the precepts. Be patient and forbearing, diligent and vigorous, of compassionate mind and single-minded, pure in fasting and precepts. In this world, doing good for one day and one night surpasses a hundred years of doing good in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Why? Because in the Land of Ultimate Bliss all beings accumulate virtue and every good, and there is not the least hair's-breadth of evil. If in this world one cultivates goodness for ten days and ten nights, the merit one gains surpasses a thousand years of doing good in the Buddha-lands of other directions. Why? Because in those Buddha-lands merit and virtue come of themselves, and there is no ground for creating evil. Only in this world is there little good and much evil; beings drink suffering and eat poison, and never cease.
(Daojin) the evils forbidden by the Buddha's Way, that is, the precepts.

[I pity you all, and with earnest heart teach and exhort you, bestowing upon you the sutras and the Dharma. Receive and hold them all, ponder them all, and practice them all. High and low, men and women, kin and friends, should in turn teach and instruct one another and mutually restrain and check themselves. Be harmonious and accord with principle, and be joyful, kind, and filial. If in what you do you transgress, then repent of your own fault. Forsake evil and draw near to good; hearing it in the morning, change by evening.
Receive and uphold the sutras and precepts as a poor man who has found a treasure.
Correct the past and cultivate the future; wash
xǐ
the mind and change your conduct. Then blessings shall come down of themselves, and whatever you wish you shall
zhé
, always)
attain.]

Out of pity for you I teach and exhort you with earnest heart, bestowing upon you the sutras and the Dharma. You should all receive them with care, ponder them, and practice them. High and low, men and women, kin and friends, should in turn teach and admonish one another and mutually restrain and check themselves (make your own mind upright, make your own body upright). Be harmonious and accord with principle, and be joyful, kind, and filial. If you transgress against the precepts, then repent of your own fault. Forsake evil and draw near to good; hearing it in the morning, change by evening. Receive and uphold the sutras and precepts as a poor man who has found a treasure. Correct the past and cultivate the future (correct the evil done in the past and diligently cultivate the good of the present and the future), wash the mind and change your conduct. Then blessings and auspiciousness shall come down of themselves, and whatever you wish shall be fulfilled.
(Fengchi jingjie) To receive and uphold the sutra means to practice according to what it says. Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing says:
“To uphold this sutra is to practice according to this sutra.” (Xifang Quezhi)

To receive and uphold the precepts means to remember and hold them without forgetting and to commit no evil. (Receive and uphold the sutras and precepts as a poor man who has found a treasure) This is the heart of this chapter, the World-Honored One's most compassionate instruction. When a poor man obtains a treasure, all his sufferings are at once stilled, and from then on he is joyful and free of care. This uses a treasure to illustrate the wondrous function of the sutras and precepts. Moreover, once a poor man has obtained a treasure, his very life depends on it, so he must guard it with all his strength and must not lose it. This exhorts the practitioner who has received the sutras and precepts to uphold them well himself, as he would guard his own life. If he transgresses, he should swiftly repent and vow never to do so again. (Sa (anciently the same as “wash”) xin yi xing) To wash away the evil thoughts in the mind and thoroughly mend one's ways. (Zhe, zhé) always.

[Wherever the Buddha goes, in states large and small, in towns and villages, none fail to receive his transforming influence. The world is harmonious and compliant, sun and moon are clear and bright. Wind and rain come in season, and disasters do not arise. The country is abundant and the people at peace, and weapons of war are of no use. Virtue is honored and benevolence is promoted, and all devote themselves to cultivating propriety and yielding. In the land there are no thieves, no wrongs or injustices. The strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds his proper place.]

Wherever the Buddha goes: states (countries), towns (cities), mounds (townships), and settlements (villages) all without exception receive the Buddha's teaching and transformation. The world is harmonious and compliant, sun and moon are clear and bright. Wind and rain come in season, and pestilence and disaster do not arise. The country is abundant and the people at peace, and there is no war. Virtue is honored and benevolence is promoted, and all devote themselves to cultivating propriety, courtesy, and yielding. In the land there are no thieves, and there are no wrongs. The strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds his proper place.

(Wherever the Buddha goes) The places the Buddha walks and reaches, that is, wherever he arrives; it also refers to the places where the Buddha-Dharma flourishes in later ages. (Mi, mǐ) none, without.

[I pity you all more than a father and mother think of their children. I have become Buddha in this world to attack evil with good and to pull out the suffering of birth and death. I cause beings to obtain the five virtues and to rise to the peace of non-activity. After I enter parinirvāṇa, the way of the sutras will gradually die out. People will become flattering and false, and will again commit every evil. The five pains and five burnings will in time grow ever more violent. You should teach and admonish one another, and according to the Buddha's sutras and Dharma, you must not transgress.]

I pity you more than a father and mother cherish their children. I have become Buddha in this world to attack evil with good and to pull out the suffering of birth and death. I cause beings to obtain the five virtues (that is, the five goods spoken of above: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol) and to enjoy the peace of non-activity. After I enter parinirvāṇa, the way of the sutras will gradually die out. People will become flattering and deceitful (fawning and treacherous) and false, and will again commit every evil. The five pains and five burnings will in time grow ever more violent. You should teach and admonish one another and strictly observe the Buddha's sutras and Dharma, and you must not transgress.

(Parinirvāṇa) rendered into Chinese as “entering extinction,” abbreviated as “nirvāṇa.” (The way of the sutras will gradually die out) Śākyamuni Buddha's True Dharma lasts five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma a thousand years, and the Final Dharma ten thousand years; when all have passed, it is called the extinction of the way of the sutras.

[Bodhisattva Maitreya joined his palms and said: The evils and sufferings of the world's people are just so, just so. The Buddha in his compassion pities them all and delivers them all. Having received the Buddha's repeated instruction, we dare not transgress or lose it.]

Bodhisattva Maitreya joined his palms and said to the Buddha: The world's people do evil and suffer, just so, just so. The Buddha in his compassion pities them all and delivers them all. Having received the Buddha's repeated instruction and encouragement, we dare not transgress or lose it.
Huimian
) instruction and encouragement.

blocks.text: 38. Bowing to the Buddha and Seeing the Land

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ānanda: If you wish to see Amitābha Buddha and the land in which the bodhisattvas, arhats, and others dwell, you should face the west, toward where the sun sets, bow in reverence, and recite “Namo Amitābha Buddha.”]

The Buddha told Ānanda: If you wish to see Amitābha Buddha and the land in which the bodhisattvas, arhats, and others dwell, you should face the west, toward where the sun sets, bow in reverence, and recite “Namo Amitābha Buddha.”

[Ānanda at once rose from his seat, faced the west with palms joined, bowed, and said: I now wish to see the Land of Ultimate Bliss and Amitābha Buddha, to make offerings and serve him, and to plant all roots of virtue.]

Ānanda at once rose from his seat, faced the west with palms joined, bowed, and said: I now wish to see the Land of Ultimate Bliss and Amitābha Buddha, to make offerings and serve him, and to plant all roots of virtue.

[In the very act of bowing, suddenly he saw the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Amitābha Buddha's countenance was vast, his bodily marks dignified and adorned, like a mountain of gold rising above all the worlds. And he heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions proclaiming and praising Amitābha Buddha's manifold virtues without obstruction and without interruption.]

In the very act of bowing, suddenly he saw the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Amitābha Buddha's countenance was vast, his bodily marks dignified and adorned, like a mountain of gold rising above all the worlds. And he heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions proclaiming and praising Amitābha Buddha's manifold virtues without obstruction and without interruption.

[Ānanda said: That Buddha's pure land is such as has never been; I too wish and delight to be born in that land. The World-Honored One said: Those born there have already drawn near to countless Buddhas and planted the roots of every virtue. If you wish to be born there, you should single-mindedly take refuge and look up in reverence.]

Ānanda said to the World-Honored One: Amitābha Buddha's pure land is so supremely adorned that I have never seen its like, and I too very much wish to be born there. The World-Honored One told Ānanda: Those born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss have already drawn near to countless Buddhas and planted the roots of every virtue. If you wish to be born there, you should single-mindedly take refuge and look up in reverence.

[While these words were being spoken, Amitābha Buddha at once emitted from the palm of his hand immeasurable light, universally illumining all the worlds of the Buddhas. Then all the Buddha-lands appeared clearly, as if they were but an arm's length away.
